title: 8  Uncertainty in quantities
section: 8.2 Where do probability distributions come from?
text:
8.2 Where do probability distributions come from?
Probability was invented in the 17th century by mathematicians interested in gambling. Progress was made by a mixture of experience reinforced by mathematical theorizing and algebraic derivation.
A significant development was the realization, in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, that the hill() function was particularly useful in the analysis of data. hill()-like distributions were observed frequently in data from diverse contexts, so much so that it came to be called the “☞ normal distribution ☜.” Mathematical theorizing, long after the normal distribution came into use, showed that in a scenario in which many independent random numbers, from whatever source, are added together, the normal distribution, or something very much like it, results. This scenario appears frequently in statistical calculations. However, over-reliance on this scenario outside statistical methodology can lead people to wrongly discount the possibility of rare events such as droughts, floods, and financial crises.
Probability distributions like the normal distribution are often used to model uncertainty. In Chapters 11 and 12, we will add a somewhat different perspective: a probability distribution is a ☞ hypothesis ☜ which we use to make sense of our experiences and observations in the world.
Starting about 1900, statisticians looked at the question of how correctly to infer properties of the real world from the results of statistical calculations. That is, they wanted to figure out what kinds of conclusions about the world are justified by analysis of data. This matter is called ☞ statistical inference ☜. One important school of thought emphasized making mathematically provable statements about inference. To do this, they had to develop a theoretical framework which came to be called ☞ frequentism ☜. Frequentist methods play a central role among statistical theorists and remain the foundation of much statistical education. Readers who have studied statistics have likely used formulas and nomenclature—e.g., p-value, hypothesis tests—that stem from the Frequentist point of view. Another framework for inference, ☞ Bayesian ☜ inference, predates Frequentism. In the Bayesian point of view, the emphasis is not on defining things in a way suitable to support mathematical proof, but rather in a way to answer questions in a form needed for quantitative reasoning, uncertainty assessment, and decision making. Over the last half-century, the Bayesian point of view has gained many adherents among statistical theorists, partly because Bayesian calculations that were once difficult became practical by using computers. In this book, we adopt the Bayesian perspective.

title: 8  Uncertainty in quantities
text:
8.3 Exemplary probability distributions
There is an infinity of probability distributions simply because there is an infinity of functions. Nevertheless, almost always modelers draw from a small library of about twenty named distributions. More precisely, these are ☞ named families of distributions ☜. Each of these families includes one or two parameters that, often, are equivalent to applying an input transformation and/or output transformation. In this section, we focus on three distributions that modelers use in everyday work: the normal, the uniform, and the exponential.

Uniform distribution

The ☞ uniform distribution ☜ models a situation where the possibilities must be within a known range, but could be anywhere in that range. Figure 8.2 shows what a uniform distribution would be for a situation like this: “She texted that she will arrive in the afternoon, but I don’t know exactly when.”
















Figure 8.2: A uniform distribution.



The parameters for the uniform distribution family are the minimum and maximum extremes of the range of possibilities.

Normal distribution

We introduced the normal distribution in Section 8.1 as the standard distribution family that corresponds to the type of uncertainty often expressed using a range or the \(\pm\) notation.


It surprises many people that these notations do not correspond to the uniform distribution. Recall that the uniform distribution labels as impossible any outcome outside of the range from minimum to maximum. However, in many circumstances, an outcome outside the range is merely unlikely, not impossible. For instance, is it impossible that our friend will arrive in the evening or before noon?
The normal distribution, on the other hand, softens the edges and replaces “impossible” with “not likely.” The further from the interval, the less likely. The closer to the center of the interval, the more likely. The normal distribution in Figure 8.3 includes the possibility that she arrived yesterday or will arrive next week. Very, very unlikely, but possible.














Figure 8.3: A normal distribution smooths out the sharp corners of Figure 8.2.



The parameters for the normal distribution set the center and spread, but are usually called the “☞ mean ☜” and “☞ standard deviation ☜.” (Some authors prefer to use “☞ variance ☜” instead of “standard deviation”: the variance is the square of the standard deviation.) The mean can be any value; the standard deviation must be positive.

Exponential distribution

The ☞ Exponential distribution ☜ corresponds to a different message from a friend. “It’s noon now. I’m going to try to get there right away. I think it will take about an hour, but I do not know anything beyond that. It might be much longer.” The exponential distribution expresses much greater uncertainty at the high end. A much more typical application would be the uncertain time between 100-year storms.
















Figure 8.4: The exponential distribution.



A concrete way to think about the exponential distribution is as a description of the intervals between randomly occurring events. In Figure 8.4, the first event was assumed to be at noon; the second event will be the time that the friend arrives. The exponential model is based on the idea that there is a fixed probability that the second event will happen in a short interval after the first. But if it doesn’t occur in that short interval, the same probability applies to the event happening in the next short interval, and so on. Perhaps contrary to intuition, this means that the probability of the second interval happening at time t after the first event decays exponentially with t, as in Figure 8.4.
The exponential model assumes that the second event is equally likely to occur at any time. There is one parameter for the distribution typically called “lambda” (which is \(\lambda\) in the Greek alphabet). The mean time between events is \(1/\lambda\). (In Figure 8.4, the mean corresponds to that for the distributions shown in Figure 8.3 and Figure 8.2.)

title: 8  Uncertainty in quantities
text:
8.4 Simulation
A relative probability distribution function takes a possible value as input and returns a number. That number is an indication of how likely that possible value is. Relative probability distributions are useful for describing uncertainty.
Often, however, we need to reason about the consequences of input uncertainty for the uncertainty in the output of the function. One technique for such reasoning with uncertainty is ☞ simulation ☜.
At the heart of simulation is the idea of using a relative probability distribution function to generate a likely input value. The input values that are associated with a high relative probability are more likely to be generated than those associated with a low relative probability.
We call the process of generating a likely input value ☞ randomly sampling from the distribution ☜ or, more generally, ☞ random number generation ☜.
For instance, in Figure 8.1, a random sample between, say, 75 and 85 would be quite likely, while sample values less than 40 would be vanishingly unlikely.
Random number generation is an important tool for many modeling applications and even plays a role in constructing the responses from AI systems. Such generators are provided for many computer languages and are often built into the language itself.
To illustrate, let’s generate a single random sample from the distribution in Figure 8.1.

rnorm(1, mean=80, sd=10)

[1] 83.92418


Generating a single number does not give much information, so modelers often generate many random numbers. We will illustrate with 20, but it’s common to generate thousands or even millions of random numbers

rnorm(20, mean=80, sd=10) |>  # The hill() distribution.
  round(digits = 1)

 [1] 68.9 72.9 73.8 88.6 80.1 59.3 67.3 79.7 71.8 74.8 82.9
[12] 65.0 77.8 92.5 95.0 89.2 74.0 85.8 75.3 59.8


As a simple example of using simulation, consider the problem posed at the start of this chapter: [-3,5]\(\times\)[-10,2].

set.seed(102)
product <- 
  runif(20, min =  -3, max = 5) * 
  runif(20, min = -10, max = 2)  
round(product, digits = 1)

 [1]   1.7  -2.5 -11.3  -3.4  15.7  -2.1 -42.2   1.9 -21.0
[10]  -1.6 -21.4   1.9 -32.8   0.0   2.7 -28.9 -25.2   0.0
[19]  -7.5 -20.2


Notice that the 20 samples of the product vary from one to the other. It is only as a group that they give us information about the uncertainty in the product. Computer graphics—with a much larger sample—makes it easy to visualize the uncertainty, as in @two-multiplied-uniforms. The distribution is not uniform, but rather has a peak in the middle and tails off to zero at the extremes.








Figure 8.5: Relative probability distribution for [-3,5] \(\times\) [-10,2] computed with 200,000 random samples.

title: 9  Composing functions
text:
9.1 Linear combinations of functions
This chapter describes tools to build custom functions. The tools help the modeler compose a function that encompasses their ideas and data about a given relationship.
To illustrate, consider this situation: a person develops a sinus infection, ending up having to go to an urgent-care clinic for treatment. An antibiotic is prescribed, the patient picks up the prescription from the pharmacy and begins taking the medication as directed: one small pill every eight hours for seven days.
Wouldn’t it be more convenient to take just one pill a day? Or why not just one pill that covers the entire week? A model can help us understand the implications of different dosing schedules.
To start, we need to know a bit about the physiology of drug absorption and elimination in the human body. The drug in the pill is absorbed through the gut over a short period of time, say, an hour. But even as the drug is being absorbed, the liver metabolizes it and removes it from the blood stream. The removal rate is proportional to the current concentration of the drug in the bloodstream; low concentration means a slow removal rate, while high concentration means a fast removal rate.
There’s no single function among our core modeling functions that captures both absorption and removal of the drug. Still, the exponential function seems a match to drug elimination. As Figure 9.1(a) shows, the exponential function with input and output scaling shows a pattern of high rate of reduction when the drug concentration is high, and low rate of reduction when the concentration is low.
The model of absorption is the hillside function with input scaling so that about half-an-hour after the pill is taken, practically all has been absorbed.
Now we are going to combine the two functions to become a reasonable model of the whole process: absorption and elimination. Drawing on past modeling experience, we’re going to multiply the two functions together, giving the overall function in Figure 9.2.
IN DRAFT: Fix the figure reference in the caption.
Although multiplying functions is a valid and powerful way to construct models, it is much more common to encounter models built by adding functions together.
Figure 9.2 depicts the concentration of a drug after taking a single pill. Let’s extend the model to cover situations where multiple pills are taken over time, as with the prescribed “one pill every 8 hours for seven days.”
With input scaling, we can adjust the time at which the pill is taken. Let’s use pill(t) to refer to the function depicted in Figure 9.2. This pill was taken at hour 0. If hour 0 is mid-night, then pill(t - 10) is the function for a pill taken at 10 am. Similarly, pill(t - 18) represents a pill taken at 6 pm. And pill(t - 26) is the next one on the schedule. and so on for the whole seven-day prescription.
The drug from each pill adds to whatever is already in the bloodstream. So the function giving the drug concentration for pills taken at 8-hour intervals (starting at 10 am on day 1) is:
all_pills <- function(t) {
  one_pill(t - 10) + one_pill(t - 18) + one_pill(t - 26) + 
  one_pill(t - 34) + one_pill(t - 42) + one_pill(t - 50) + 
  one_pill(t - 58) # ... and so on.
}
All_pills(t) is an example of a ☞ linear combination of functions ☜. Here, the functions being combined are all input-shifted version of the same pill(t) function, but linear combinations can involve any functions. Figure 9.3 shows all_pills() over the first two-and-a-half days of the prescription.
Figure 9.3: Concentration of a medicine in the bloodstream of a person who takes a pill every 8 hours, starting at 10 am on day 1.
Figure 9.3 shows how each additional pill raises the drug concentration. Suppose the pharmacist’s goal is to maintain at all times a drug concentration above the therapeutic level of 1 mg/liter, providing no respite to the bacteria causing the infection.
Compare the situation in Figure 9.4 to that of Figure 9.2. A single pill per day regimen would result in the drug concentration falling below 1 mg/liter for most of the day. That’s not acceptable. The most obvious fix comes from recognizing that pill every 8 hours is three pills a day. So to be fair, the comparison the daily pill should have three times the dose of the 8-hour pill. Taking this into account, will the one-pill-per-day regimen work if we tripled the dose of each pill?
This situation also falls under the aegis of the linear combination technique. In linear combinations, the modeler is free to set the output scale the functions being combined. For the one-dose-per-day plan (at triple the dose) the model of drug concentration looks like this:
once_per_day <- function(t) {
  3 * one_pill(t - 10) + 3 * one_pill(t - 34) + 
    3 * one_pill(t - 58) # ... and so on
}
Let’s graph the function:
Figure 9.4: Drug concentration over time when taking one pill per day at triple the dose. The drug concentration falls below the therapeutic dose (the magenta line) for almost half of each day.
The process of exponential decay, which we used in our model of drug concentration, is so familiar throughout science and engineering that it was not surprising to pharmacologists to observe the pattern with drug elimination. The model used in this section uses a drug half-life—the amount of time it takes for the value of the function to fall by half—of about 4.5 hours. Naturally, the half-life can vary from drug to drug. When figuring out what dose should be used in a pill and how often it should be taken, scientists used experiment and statistics to determine the therapeutic dose and the drug half-life.
It turns out that the method of linear combinations is well suited to constructing model functions from data, not just in biomedicine but in all manner of social science and economics contexts.

title: 9  Composing functions
text:
9.2 Linear regression
[In everyday speech, the word “regression” means a return to a previous, less advanced, or worse state.
A linear combination is a mathematical idea: a way to build new functions by combining existing functions. This is in not at all the meaning of the word in the phrase “linear regression.” We arrived at this confusing situation by historical accident. The original usage in statistics in the 1890s reflected a misconception that treated a simple mathematical pattern as if it emerged from an underlying natural, biological, or economic process. History can be sticky; our modern understanding is better captured by the name ☞ linear modeling ☜.]{.column-margin} Very often, however, the point of building a new function is to represent data, constructing a function that captures the patterns seen in the data. The technique for using data to inform the construction of a linear combination is traditionally called ☞ linear regression ☜.
The same() and flat() core modeling functions are the most common building blocks for linear regression models, but in principle any function can be included in a linear regression. And, linear regression effectively automates the process of output scaling introduced in Section 7.2.
Let’s use an example to set the stage for understanding linear regression/modeling. Suppose you are studying the factors that contribute to student performance in elementary school. Teachers like to think of themselves as the critical factor, but also point to the benefits of small class sizes and supportive family environments. It’s easy to imagine a system where teacher performance in the classroom is carefully observed and scored by experts, although genuine experts are always in short supply. But, for our example, let’s operationalize teacher skill using such a performance evaluation. Class size is easy to operationalize: count the students in each class and average over each student’s classes.
Supportive family environments? This is harder. We are all inspired by stories of undereducated parents pushing their children to succeed against the odds. Operationalizing this dimension (these dimensions?) requires identifying measurable indicators. Two such are the parents’ level of education and the family’s income. (Perhaps it’s really lack of income that matters, since low-income families often face significant challenges.)
Operationalizing student performance can be controversial, but for this example let’s simply use the score on a standardized test.
We refer to “inputs” and “output” to be consistent with the nomenclature used in this book to describe functions. In statistics texts, the phrases “predictors” or “explanatory variables” are often used instead of “inputs,” and “response variable” is often used instead of “output.” In economics, it’s common to use the terms “independent variables” and “dependent variable.”
We’ve identified four input quantities: teacher performance, parent’s education, family income, and class size. We want to build a function that translates these four inputs into the one output: standardized test score. What should that function look like?
Linear regression involves basing the construction of the function using data. For the example, let’s imagine a data frame where the specimen is an individual student in grade 5 and the columns correspond to the input quantities (performance, education, income, size) and the output (score).
Typically, as in this example, the input quantities have different dimension and are measured in different units. For example, in this example, income is measured in dollars (dimension W), education in years of schooling (dimension T), performance as a score on an evaluation (dimension [1]), and size as the number of students in a class (also dimension [1]).  The output quantity, score, also has dimension [1] and its own units.There are many scales for measuring school performance. When we talk about them, we don’t typically give a unit name. For instance, a score of”600 on the SAT math test,” which is roughly equivalent to a score of “25 on the ACT text,” or a “gradepoint of 3.5.”
A linear combination is an ideal format for combining input quantities with different dimensions. It is a generalization of the output scaling introduced in Chapter 7 which we used to convert the pure-number output of the core modeling functions to an output quantity with dimension and units. For our example, the function might be written this way:


score_model <- 
  function(performance, education, income, size) {
    A * performance + 
    B * education + 
    C * income + 
    D * size +
    E
}

The quantity A is a conversion factor that turns performance into a quantity that has the same units and dimension as score. Similarly, B converts years of education into a score and so on for C, D, and E.  These conversion factors are called ☞ coefficients ☜.Another word for “coefficient” is ☞ scalar ☜. This name is a reminder that the point is to “scale” something.
We can figure out the units and dimension of each of the coefficients using the conversion factor ideas from Chapter 3. For instance, the C coefficient has to turn income (dimension W) into a score (dimension [1]), so its dimension would be [1] / W. Even more, we can say what are the units of C: if income is measured in dollars and score is measured in SAT points, then the units of C would be SAT points per dollar.
Knowing the units and dimensions of the coefficients helps, but it does not directly tell what the numerical value of the quantity should be. This is where the method of linear regression comes in: to find the numerical values of the coefficients that best match the observed data. The calculations themselves are based on theory beyond the scope of this book, but that poses no problem at all since linear regression is implemented in software that anyone can use. IN DRAFT: Some computing skill development exercises demonstrate how.
Given that software finds the values of the coefficients, the modeler can focus on two critical tasks:

Identifying the relevant input and output quantities for the model.
Interpreting the coefficients and what they tell us about the workings of the system being modeled.

These two tasks are intimately related . Let’s start with (2).
Each of the coefficients on an input is not just a rate (for instance SAT-points/dollar for C); it is also a rate of change. In other words, the coefficient tells us how much the model output quantity changes when the input quantity changes by one unit. In the example, each of the four coefficients A, B, C, and D is a rate of change that quantifies how the model output will change with a unit change in the corresponding model input. All the terms in the linear combination add together, giving the total change in the model output as a result of changes in all the inputs.
One consequence of this is that each coefficient has meaning only within the context set by the other coefficients. If the modeler were to change the input quantities (for example, leaving out teacher performance), the numerical value of each of the other coefficients would also likely change.
Sadly, even as of the 2020s, mainstream introductory statistics courses often fail to adequately teach students about the context-dependent nature of regression coefficients and the importance of specifying which input quantities are included in a model.
This mathematical fact accounts for many of the disputes one hears about in research results. Different researchers who use different input quantities in their models, even when using the same data for fitting, will get their own coefficients that can seem in conflict with those found by other researchers.
In reporting research results, the phrases ☞ after adjusting for ☜ or ☞ holding constant ☜, or ☞ controlling for ☜ are used to signal which input quantities are used in the model. This is critical information.

title: 9  Composing functions
text:
9.3 Function graphics
One function that we live with every day is the terrain around us: elevation as a function of latitude and longitude. There is a well-accepted graphical format for showing terrain: the topographical map. Figure 9.5 shows an example: the terrain of an island.






Figure 9.5: 1958 US Geological Survey topographical map of St. John in the US Virgin Islands in the Caribbean Sea. Source



The topographical map has many curved lines, called contours. These are easiest to see for the part of the scene that is covered by water. There, the contours are thin blue lines. Each such line traces a path that maintains the same depth.
On land, the contours are brown and are very closely spaced. Here, each contour depicts where the elevation is at a constant elevation above sea level. Many of the contours are labeled. On land, the label gives the elevation; in the sea, the label gives the depth of the water. The map also labels with a number the elevation of a few outstanding points such as the peak of hills or the depth of undersea bowls.
It takes practice to learn how to extract information from topographical maps. Let’s get started by focussing on the terrain around Hansen Bay, just to the left of center on the map. The shoreline is marked as a blue curve. More important for our purposes, that blue curve is a contour line that marks elevation 0, at sea level. You can trace the contour around the island: it never goes inland or out to sea. Moving inland, there are several more contours pretty much parallel to the shoreline and to each other. On this map, each successive contour is at a higher elevation than the one previous; the elevation difference between adjacent contours is 40 feet. Walking inland from Hansen Bay toward Nancy Hill, you cross four light brown contours until you arrive a darker brown one. That darker brown contour indicates an elevation of 200 feet above sea level. (If you trace the dark brown contour around the island, you will find a label on it: 200.) Continuing toward Nancy Hill, you cross another 4 light-brown contours then, having ascended another 200 feet, alight on a dark-brown one circling Nancy Hill. The dark-brown contour marks an elevation of 200 + 200 = 400 feet above sea level. Continuing to climb from the 400 foot contour toward the peak, you cross one, two, and a third contour barely visible under the marker for the peak. We have reached 200 + 200 + 120 = 520 feet when we reach the last, highest contour. The peak is just a little higher: marked as 523 feet on the map.
The contours tell you more about the terrain than the elevation at each point. For example, the steepest route up from any given point is perpendicular to the contour through that point. Steep areas of terrain have closely spaced contours. Conversely, areas with widely spaced contours are relatively flat, as you can see along the shoreline of Hansen Bay. Naturally, the steepness of a path depends on which direction the path goes. Paths perpendicular to contours are steep, paths parallel to contours are flat. With this in mind, look at the road that links Hansen Bay to Princess Creek in the far northwest corner of the map. Roads are generally designed to avoid going steeply uphill, and you can see that the Princess Creek/Hansen Bay road tends to follow the contours, crossing obliquely at shallow angles rather than cutting straight up the steepest slopes.
Or consider the narrow neck connecting the two larger landmasses. This is marked “haul over,” which makes sense because the path connecting the south side of the next to the north side does not cross any contours. That path is relatively flat, a good route to haul a boat overland between the two sides.
The equivalent of a topographical map for functions is called a ☞ contour plot ☜. The output of the function corresponds to the elevation in the map, two inputs play the roles of latitude and longitude respectively. A contour plot provides a mechanism to read off the output for given values of the inputs, but the skilled interpreter can glean more information than that. Figure 9.6 shows an example, the heat-index function introduced in Chapter 6. The inputs are temperature and humidity; the output is the heat index.
Panel (a) of Figure 9.6 shows the function in tabular form, just as it was presented in the 1979 paper that introduced the heat index. Given values for the temperature and humidity, you can easily find the corresponding output from the table.
Panel (b) shows the heat index function as a contour plot. By avoiding the table’s visual clutter of a grid of numbers, some simple patterns can be seen. For instance, consider on (b) the heat index output for input temperatures lower than 30°C; the contours run in parallel with a slight upward slope from left to right.
Such parallel contours correspond to the function being a linear combination of the inputs. The slope means that the function increases with both dry-bulb temperature and relative humidity. That the slope is shallow means that—at least in the top portion of the graphical space—the function hardly depends on humidity.
Now consider dry-bulb temperatures higher than 30°C, especially for humidities greater than, say, 50%. The contours are still parallel but they are heavily inclined from left to right and closely spaced together.
The close spacing of the contours indicates, as in the topographical map of Figure 9.5, the function is very steep: a small change in either input produces a large change in the output. This relationship is what’s behind the common summertime complaint: “It’s not the heat, it’s the humidity.”
The inclination of the contours tells us something else: the heat index for high ambient temperatures is closely linked to both humidity and temperature. And the curvature of the contour lines indicates an interaction between temperature and humidity.



Figure 9.6: Two graphical presentations of the heat index function. Panel (b) has been drawn with an upside-down vertical axis, the better to correspond the tabular convention of increasing values from top to bottom.







As a table







As a contour plot







The explanation for the big change in pattern from top to bottom on the plot is physiological, not meteorological. Keep in mind that human core body temperature is 37°C. Metabolism generates heat and the core temperature would go up above 37°C if it were not for the body’s cooling mechanisms. When a lot of heat is being generated, as in exercise, one of these cooling mechanisms becomes evident: sweating. Sweating is most effective at low humidities. At high humidities, the evaporation of sweat is less efficient, leading to a rapid increase in perceived heat, which is captured by the steep contours in the heat index plot.
A heat index of 37°C leaves no way for the body to dissipate metabolic heat. Consequently, the core body temperature starts to go up. You can see from the function output that a heat index of 37°C corresponds to dry-bulb temperatures around 42°C, so long as the humidity is low. But as humidity increases, the safety mechanism of sweating shorts out and the skin temperature rises quickly.
A heat index of 65°C or thereabouts is thought to be the limit of human tolerance. After a few hours of exposure at this level the risk of death is very high. At high humidities, this fatal threshold is reached even when the ambient dry-bulb temperature is near normal body temperature.

title: 10  Trade-offs
text:
10.1 Optimization
The everyday verb “trade” involves exchanging one thing for another. Buying lunch is a trade: you exchange money for food. Almost always, such an exchange involves two parties, in this case a buyer and a seller. A ☞ trade-off ☜ is a kind of trade that involves only one party who has to balance competing objectives. A person who decides to buy a cheaper lunch in order to have money for a movie faces a trade-off between the quality of the food and the amount of money available for entertainment.
Trade-offs often involve money, but not always. For instance, a painter bending far from a ladder to get to that last little bit of unpainted third-story window trim is trading off efficiency for safety. Another painter, who climbs down and moves the ladder closer to the window, faces the same trade-off but evaluates it differently. The second painter is prioritizing safety over efficiency.
This chapter is about describing trade-offs and some of the ideas that can be used to deal with them quantitatively.
“Optimization” is a mathematical topic that deals with finding the best from a set of possible choices. There are many technical situations in which optimization techniques are useful. An example is calculating the coefficients used in linear regression. But optimization is also used, importantly, in routing and logistics, for example finding the best sequence of stops for a delivery van or the layout of transistor circuits on an integrated silicon chip.
In a trade-off, the existence or meaning of “best” is not clear-cut. Still, some of the terminology from optimization is useful for describing trade-offs quantitatively.
Optimization can involve one or more objective functions, although most mathematics courses emphasize the single-objective case. Optimization with a single objective function is a good way to introduce the basic concepts and terminology, but trade-offs typically involve multiple objective functions.
An objective function is a perfectly ordinary function along the lines discussed in Chapter 6 or Chapter 9. The modeler constructs an objective function to capture a particular goal in the optimization problem. For instance, apartment hunting can be seen as an optimization problem where the input domain is the list of available apartments for rent. One typical objective is to maximize the square footage of the apartment, others are to minimize the rent and distance to work, and to maximize the quality of the neighborhood, etc. These are four different objectives and each is represented by its own objective function. In this case, the modeler building the objective functions would assemble a table over each of the available apartments with each objective function being a column in the table. For instance, square footage would be one column, rent another, and so on.
The term “objective function” is properly descriptive. In optimization problems one has some goal in mind—the objective, the output of the function—and seeks to select an input value that will produce the largest value of that output.
Optimization problems sometimes involve situations where the goal is to minimize rather than maximize the output. Any minimization problem can be turned into a maximization problem by putting a minus sign in front of the objective function.
The “solution” to the optimization problem is the input value that achieves this maximum (or minimum) output. The output achieved is called the objective function’s ☞ maximum ☜ or ☞ minimum ☜, depending on the context, but the point is to find the input value that produces it. Such an input could be reasonably called the “optimum input,” but the technical name for it is the ☞ argmax ☜. For a minimization problem, the corresponding word is ☞ argmin ☜.
“Argmax” and “argmin” are not ordinary English words; they are syllabic abbreviations, like FedEx (short for Federal Express), formed from the first syllables of words in a phrase. The phrase relevant to optimization is “the argument that produces the maximum output value.” Keep in mind that “argument” in this phrase is used as a synonym for “input.”
Figure 10.1 shows the argmax for two example objective functions. Those functions each have an output that varies with its input. In the spirit of fun, we imagine that the output in panel (a) is the taste score assigned to a baked item and, for (b), the relative probability of locating a shipwreck. However, the output scale does not matter at all to the optimization problem. The argmax is merely the input that produces the maximum output.
To judge from panel (a), the tastiest baking temperature for the item is 315 °F. As for the shipwreck, its most likely position is (122 W, 7.4 N), but the relative probability there is not much higher than at areas within about \(\pm 1\) degree of longitude and latitude. In each panel, the blue dot marks the input value, not the output value.
How does one find the argmax? If you have a graph, look at it, find the point in the picture that corresponds to the peak of the hill and read off the input values for that point.
It is hard to construct useful graphics when the objective function has three or more inputs. Optimization problems with many inputs can be solved with a different technique, which we will discuss in Chapter 16. In training AI models, the objective function literally can have billions of inputs.
The technique for finding an argmax can be implemented in software. This fact lowers the priority to the student of learning mathematical theory of optimization. The real questions one faces in optimization are how to develop a model for the objective function and whether there is an argmax at all.

title: 10  Trade-offs
text:
10.2 Toward trade-offs
Often, the purpose of finding an argmax is to guide a decision or choice. In Figure 10.1(a), the choice involves setting the oven temperature to produce the tastiest cake. In (b), the choice is where to start searching for the sunken wreck.
Sometimes, however, the proposed objective function does not capture all relevant considerations. In such cases, the argmax of an objective function may not guide a good decision. For instance, consider the objective function in Figure 10.2 that takes an automobile’s speed as input and produces as output the time until the car reaches its destination. This is a minimization problem, since we want to take the least time possible to get to the destination.








Figure 10.2: Time in hours to a destination 100 km away as a function of car speed. To minimize time to destination, a higher speed is better.





Figure 10.2 shows the objective function. Naturally, the faster the car goes, the less time it takes to reach the destination. We’ve marked the argmin near 120 km/h on the graphics input scale, but mathematically any input larger than this would result in an even better (lower) output, which is the meaning of the blue arrow. Keep in mind that the blue annotation corresponds to an argmin, even though it is at a high speed. Remember: The “min” in argmin refers to the output of the objective function, not the input. The “minimum” is the about the output of the function, the “argmin” is about the input that generates the minimum output.
The optimization result—the argmin being at a high speed, i.e., go as fast as possible—violates any driver’s common sense. The problem is that the model has only one objective: minimizing time to destination. Any responsible driver will incorporate additional objectives into the decision-making process. Let’s list some of these:

minimize time to destination
maximize safety
maximize fuel efficiency
minimize legal violations

Each of these objective functions, when considered in isolation, has its own argmax or argmin, depending on whether the output of the function is to be maximized or minimized.

Time to destinationArgmin: Go as fast as possible.
Safety: Argmax: Drive at a safe speed. If there is traffic, a safe speed will be similar to other cars on the road. If no traffic, heed visibility and road conditions.
Fuel efficiency:Argmax: Look up the most fuel-efficient speed for your car on a trustworthy web site. On a windless day, this is likely to be around 80 km/h (50 mph).
Lawfulness: Argmin: Keep speed at or under the legal speed limit.

Depending on conditions, the objective functions can be in conflict with one another. For instance, when traffic is exceeding the speed limit, the safety goal conflicts with the legal compliance goal. Each of the goals (2), (3), and (4) conflict with (1).
Such conflicting objectives are the origin of trade-offs.

title: 10  Trade-offs
text:
10.3 Resolving trade-offs
A key feature of an unresolved trade-off is that the outputs of the various objective functions are ☞ incommensurate ☜ with each other. If they were commensurate, we could simply add the outputs of the various objective functions together, to produce a single objective functions, a situation giving an easy answer.
An important quantitative approach to trade-offs is to find conversion factors to transform the output from each objective function into a common unit, allowing for direct comparison and aggregation. (As we will see, the conversion factors are called shadow prices.)
Drivers deal with the driving-speed trade-off in the previous section every day using intuition or heuristics. One important heuristic here is “obey the speed limit.” By way of justification for the heuristic, a driver might argue that the speed limit is set based on safety considerations and, since the government has an interest in reducing fuel consumption, is likely close to the optimal speed for efficiency. Another heuristic is “follow the flow of traffic,” which is particularly valuable when the flow of traffic exceeds the posted speed limit. And in special circumstances—snow, ice, dense fog—even the flow of traffic may not be a good guide.
It’s unlikely that a careful quantitative analysis would provide better guidance than the heuristics already in use. But I want to draw on the driving situation to illustrate what mathematical approaches are available to guide decision-making in general. Using a non-controversial issue as the example—driving—frees us from the preconceptions, political, and ethical stances that often complicate discussions in other domains, such as health care, government spending policies, and environmental regulations.
Even if we do not perceive the four objectives in highway driving as active elements in our everyday choices, a simple thought experiment can reveal that each would be deemed important under changed circumstances.
For instance, suppose that fuel costs went up by a factor of 100, that is, that gasoline cost about $400 US per gallon (approximately $100 per liter). The fuel-related cost of driving a mile would increase from about 15 cents per mile to about $15 per mile. We can construct a small model to quantify the implications of this. Supposing that a highway speed reduction from 60 mph to 40 mph reduces fuel consumption by, say, 20%. Travel time on a previously 1 hour trip (60 miles at 60 mph) would increase to 1.5 hours (60 miles at 40 mph): a 30-minute increase in travel time. This time increase is offset by the savings on fuel. At $4 per gallon fuel cost, the 20% reduction in fuel use would save 3 cents per mile, or $1.80 over the 60-mile trip. Judge for yourself whether a savings of $1.80 is worth the extra 30 minutes of travel time. I think most people would say no. At the higher fuel costs, the savings would be $180. I suspect most people would gladly exchange 30 minutes of their time for $180.
You might discard this observation on the grounds that the hypothetical 100-fold increase in fuel costs is unrealistic. That people would change their behavior in this extreme scenario, however, is a signal that drivers are sensitive to fuel costs. Think for yourself whether a $90 savings would be worth the 30 minutes. Or perhaps $45 would be worth it, or even $15. If so, we don’t need the 100-fold increase to make the point; an 8-fold increase is all that’s required.
Now consider a scenario in which a zero-tolerance policy to speeding is adopted. Any violation of the speed limit would lead to a suspension of your driver’s license. Would this change your driving behavior? Most likely it would. (At least until the next election when the people responsible for the policy would be thrown out of office).
To simplify the discussion, Figure 10.3 imagines an optimization context with two objective functions, Score() and Savings(). The input to each is a policy measure (analogous to the speed you choose to drive). For easier comparison between the two functions, they have been overlaid on the same plot. For each function, the argmax is an input value, that is, a point on the horizontal axis. The two functions have different argmaxes. And there are different vertical scales, one applying to Score and the other to Savings. Note that the vertical scales differ not just in amount but in dimension: one is a “Score in points” and the other is a “Savings in tons.”








Figure 10.3: Two objective functions whose outputs have different dimension. For later reference, a handful of values of the policy measure input are marked with letters. For instance, policy D corresponds to an input value 3.





If Score() were the only objective function, we would set the policy measure to 3, the argmax for Score(). Similarly, if Savings() were the only objective function, we would set the policy measure to 5, the argmax for Savings().
It would be handy to add the two objective functions together to produce a single function whose argmax can be conclusively found. But the outputs of the two objective functions are stated with different dimensions and units: score is in points while savings is in tons. That is, the two outputs are incommensurate. As described in Chapter 3, addition is not a valid operation when quantities have different dimensions. (A hint about what is to come: Division is valid even when the quantities have different dimensions.)
But if both objectives in Figure 10.3 are worthy of consideration, setting the policy measure at the argmax of one leads to a seriously suboptimal outcome for the other objective.
Let’s switch to another graphical format to illustrate the trade-off. In Figure 10.3 the horizontal axis the the policy measure, that is, the input to the objective problems. The two vertical axes correspond to the output of the two objective functions—Score() and Savings()—one axis for each function.
In Figure 10.4 we re-arrange the axes. First, we delete entirely the horizontal input axis and represent the input value as the position along a curve. For clarity, Figure 10.3 we marked with letters nine different input values. Those same letters appear in Figure 10.4 as locations along the curve. But the axes for Figure 10.4 are re-arranged versions of the two vertical axes from Figure 10.3. Each point on the curve shows the output of the Score and Savings function for one input value. For example, for the input value A, the position on the curve marked with A is based on the Score value for input A and the Savings value for input A.
From Figure 10.4, what can we say about which choice is the best? It’s important to keep in mind that each of the objective functions in Figure 10.3 is for a maximization problem. So bigger outputs are better. From the axes, you might translate this into a simple rule: move as far as possible to the north-east. But this isn’t right.








Figure 10.4: Illustration of the trade-off between two objectives: score() and savings().





Figure 10.4 lets us compare any two input choices, say D versus E or A versus B. In order to claim that one of the labeled choices is better than the other, we need the outcome on both graphical axes to be better for one choice than for the other. For instance, both the Score and the Savings are larger at input B than at input A. Choice B is therefore better in all respects than choice A. In contrast, when comparing D versus E, we see that E has a larger Savings but it also has a smaller Score.
When comparing two inputs, as with A and B, if one is better in all respects—here this means better both in Score and in Savings—we say that one choice ☞ dominates ☜ the other. B dominates A.
We can compare any two input levels in this way. For instance, F dominates G because it has higher Savings and a higher Score. And D dominates C for the same reason. But we cannot demonstrate that F dominates D or vice versa; each is strong on one axis but weak on the other.
Since F dominates G, H, and I, we can eliminate those choices; they are sub-optimal. Similarly, D dominates C, B, and A, eliminating those as sensible choices.
Deleting all the dominated inputs, what’s left? Any choice from F through E to D.
Here is another, more human oriented way to look at the situation. Suppose we have two people, one a big fan of setting the policy measure to 8, that is, favoring option I. The other is more moderate and prefers option F. Now they are presented with the objective functions in Figure 10.3. The F-advocate can make a compelling argument to the I-advocate. Moving from I to F will accomplish both objectives better; a win-win outcome.
If the competition were between partisans of F, E, and D, however, the win-win argument doesn’t apply. To convince the F-partisans to move toward E (or further along, to D), the E-partisan would have to acknowledge that the increased outcome for Score (by about 22 points) would come at the cost of a decrease in the outcome for Savings (by about 8 tons).
Another way to say this is that there is a price for Score in terms of Savings. Usually, a price is a ratio of money per item, e.g. $2.89 per apple. Note that in a price, the item purchased is on the bottom of the ratio. And the top quantity does not have to be money; it could be tons of Savings. In this situation, switching between F and E entails a gain of 8 tons of Savings at the loss (that is, cost) of 22 points in Score. As a price for Score, this is 8/22 = 0.36 tons per point. This ratio is called the ☞ shadow price ☜. The word price is appropriate by analogy to the things we buy, measured as money per unit of the goods purchased, as in $4 per gallon of gasoline.
Whenever there is the possibility of an exchange, a price is the quantitative indicator to help determine whether the exchange is worthwhile. You wouldn’t buy a shirt if it were, in your opinion, too expensive. You get to make this choice, but knowing the price helps to make the decision criterion more clear.

title: 10  Trade-offs
section: 10.4 Case study: Shadow prices in tuberculosis control
text:
10.4 Case study: Shadow prices in tuberculosis control
Paul Farmer (1959–2022) was an anthropologist and physician, and famously a co-founder of Partners in Health, an organization dedicated to providing high-quality healthcare to impoverished communities around the world. A particular emphasis to PIH is the treatment of tuberculosis. Farmer both developed and advocated for the treatment of multi-drug resistant (MDR) tuberculosis, which is notably more difficult and expensive to treat than standard tuberculosis. He marshalled many arguments to allocate funds to MDR treatment, including ones about human rights and the risk of untreated MDR tuberculosis spreading within communities.
In 1998, at a meeting of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, Farmer made the case to an audience of physicians, scientists, and policymakers. One member of the audience, Russian physician Alex Goldfarb, offered another perspective on the issue, drawing on his experience managing tuberculosis programs to treat Russian prison inmates. As recounted in Tracy Kidder’s 2003 biography of Farmer, Mountains beyond Mountains (p. 162), Goldfarb described his dilemma:

“I want to share with you a simple reality. I have six million dollars. With three million dollars I can implement DOTS [a standard treatment, but not effective for MDR] for five thousand prison inmates. And assuming that ten percent have MDR-TB, forty-five hundred will be cured and five hundred will go down with MDR-TB and die. There’s nothing much you can do. So, I have a choice. And my choice is to use another three million dollars to treat the five hundred with MDR-TB, or go to another region and treat another five thousand. I’m working with limited resources. So my choice is not involved in the human rights of five-hundred people, but five-hundred people versus five thousand people. And this is a very practical question for me, because I have six million dollars. And the second question is that if I disclose to the Russian people that I spent six thousand dollars per case in MDR-TB in the prisons with tens of thousands of people dying all around, they will tell me that I am building a golden palace for a selected few. So for those of us who have to make those decisions with limited resources, it’s a very serious question.”

Clearly, one objective in this situation is to save lives. More lives saved is better: a maximization problem. The other, competing objective in the situation is indicated by the phrase, “I’m working with limited resources.” Seen one way, this is a simple statement of fact. But the fact emerges because an objective of the body that makes decisions about funding is to minimize the amount of money spent.
If the only objective was to minimize money spent, the decision would be straightforward: don’t spend any money at all on MDR-TB, spend it on other needs. Or, If the only objective was to maximize the number of lives saved by treatment, the decision is equally straightforward: spend as much money as needed to save as many lives as possible. This would, of course, draw money away from other needs. The trade-off exists because we are trying to accomplish both objectives at the same time.
The numbers given by Goldfarb indicate a shadow price of $3,000,000 per forty-five hundred cured patients, or roughly $667 per life saved from non-MDR tuberculosis. This is a tragically low price, which points to a harsh and grossly unfair allocation of resources in the broader Russian economy and prison system. Still, Goldfarb can do little about the broad situation; he has to work within the constraints of his limited budget. His choice, buy non-MDR lives at $667 per life versus buying MDR lives at $6,000 per life, still low, but much higher than $667 per life.
What would you do, instead?

title: 11  Hypothesis and likelihood
text:
11.1 The likelihood framework
We build models based on our understanding of the systems being modeled. Naturally, this understanding is not perfect. Indeed, there can be honest dispute about how a system operates and what factors are most important in influencing its behavior.
In many (most?) settings, it is not realistic to expect the modeler to get things right the first time, or even after several tries. Effective modelers treat their work as an application of the ☞ scientific method ☜, iteratively refining their models based on insight and evidence.
Such refinement depends on the ability to compare models to one another and pick the better one. In the language of Chapter 10, we might call this finding an “optimal” model. We will do this by developing an objective function that takes competing models as input and returns as output a numerical measure of each model’s performance.
The method is standard in many areas of science, technology, commerce, and any field where decisions must be taken. The standard terminology, however, is not usually about comparing models. The word used most often is “hypothesis.” The two words—“model” and “hypothesis”—are closely related. Every model is a formalized implementation of a hypothesis about how the system being modeled works.
There are many definitions for the word hypothesis. Often, the definitions emphasize the ☞ scientific method ☜, one description of which is called the ☞ hypothetico-deductive method ☜, as described here. In the context of the scientific method, a reasonable definition for “hypothesis” is along the lines of the following, offered by an AI prompted to define “hypothesis” specifically in the context of the scientific method:
We often think of hypotheses (and the models that implement them) as developing over time, as implied by the phrase “further investigation.” But for the purposes of comparing and competing hypotheses, a better picture is that of a set of models all present at the same time, like the candidates in an election.
To choose the best among the hypotheses, we need to be able to compare them to one another in terms of their ability to account for observed data and make accurate predictions. The numerical measure, the output of our objective function, is a quantity called ☞ likelihood ☜.
Chapter 8 discussed how to use probability distributions to quantify uncertainty. Section 2 introduced a Bayesian notion of where probability distributions come from: they are hypotheses concocted by humans.
In the ☞ likelihood framework ☜, we replace ideas about individual hypotheses being correct or incorrect, right or wrong, true or false. Instead, we consider collections of hypotheses, putting them into competition with one another, just as sports playoffs pit different athletes or teams against one another. In sports, a higher score gives a team a claim to being better than the opponent.
In the likelihood framework, the competing entities are hypotheses represented by probability distributions about the relative probability of each possible observed outcome. The “score” for each competing hypothesis is the “☞ likelihood ☜.” And just as sports teams compete in a particular setting—a game or match—hypotheses compete in a setting: data.
The reader who has never heard of “likelihood” in this sense may wonder if the framework is the right or best one for placing hypotheses into competition. We turn to the field of statistics to answer. As described in Section 2, Bayesian and Frequentist statisticians fundamentally disagree. Despite their conflicting stances, both camps put likelihood at the center of their methodologies.
To illustrate how likelihood works, consider how to model uncertainty in the time interval between major events, for example, the time between economic depressions or the time between magnitude 6.5+ earthquakes in a region.
To be specific, suppose we have data on the timing of the last five events of some kind: events occurred in 1905, 1919, 1950, 1973, and 1990. We would like to model the uncertainty in the timing of the next event based on these observations. We have information on five observed intervals between consecutive events. Four of them are definite: 14 years between 1905 and 1919, 31 years between 1919 and 1950, 23 years between 1950 and 1973, and 17 years between 1973 and 1990. The fifth interval, between 1990 and the next event, is unknown. This doesn’t mean that we have no information about it. At this time of this writing, 2027, we know the fifth interval is at least 37 years long.
The standard model for the interval between random events is the exponential distribution. This has one parameter, the rate. A good choice of rate is the one most consistent with the data. Likelihood provides the measure of consistency between a hypothesized rate and the observed intervals. The exponential function Figure 11.1 shows the likelihood of any one interval observation for a hypothesized rate of 0.03. Each of the observed intervals, 14, 17, 23, and 31 years has been marked in the graph.
Figure 11.1: The likelihood for any observed interval under the hypothesis of an exponential distribution with rate 0.03. The four completed intervals by vertical lines. The likelihood of each is printed beside the vertical line.
The likelihood for each individual observation is the value of the likelihood function at that observation. For instance, the likelihood of an interval of 14 years is 0.0197. When there are multiple observations, we need to combine their likelihoods. How to accomplish this?
The answer comes from the same feature of probability arithmetic that you may have encountered in games (or in math classes about games). For instance, the probability of rolling a 5 with a die is 1/6. The probability of rolling a 5 twice in a row involves combining the individual probabilities by multiplication: 1/6 \(\times\) 1/6 = 1/36.
The overall likelihood of our four observations—intervals of 14, 17, 23, and 31 years—is the product of their individual likelihoods: #\(0.0197 \times 0.0180 \times 0.0150 \times 0.0118 = 6.325e-8\ .\)$ This number is very small in magnitude. That’s because there are very many other possibilities for the intervals that could have been observed, say, 12, 19, 24, 28 and such. Since there are so many similar sets of numbers, the likelihood of observing any particular one is small. As you’ll see, the ultimate use of likelihoods is to compare them one to another, that is, to compare their relative size.
If all we had were the four completed intervals, the overall likelihood of 6.325e-8 would be the value we assign to the specific hypothesis of an exponential distribution with a rate parameter of 0.03. We are going to put this specific hypothesis into a competition for the best hypothesis. As described in Chapter 10, to define “best,” we need an objective function whose input will be the rate parameter and whose output will be the overall likelihood of our observed data—14, 17, 23, and 31 years—under that hypothesis.
By carrying out the same calculations we did for a rate of 0.03, we can find the likelihood for other rates. These are displayed in Table 11.1. The workflow is this, for each row:
This is repeated for each hypothesized rate. For the sake of conciseness, Table 11.1 shows only five hypothesized rates. See Figure 11.2 for a more complete picture.
From the overall likelihood for each of the hypothesized rate parameters shown in Table 11.1, we can see that a rate of 0.05 /year is more likely than our original hypothesis of 0.03 / year. But we can say more. The likelihood ratio comparing the 0.05 per year hypothesis to the 0.03 per year hypothesis is 1.41. Table 11.2, to be introduced in the next section, translates likelihood ratios into verbal statements of relative support. A likelihood ratio of 1.41 is really “no evidence” in favor of 0.05 per year versus 0.03 per year. The reason for this wimpy result is that four observations is a tiny amount of data.
If we can’t argue for the 0.05 per year hypothesis over the 0.03 per year hypothesis based on the four complete observations, what possible hypotheses can we rule out. To illustrate this, we’re going to extend the calculations shown in Table 11.1 to a wider range of intervals and plot the results in Figure 11.2.
Panel (a) shows the likelihood function for the four complete intervals, the same calculation as in Table 11.1.
Panel (b) is the likelihood function for the incomplete interval, that is, an interval that is still ongoing after 37 years from 1990 to 2027. If the rate parameter were very low, say one event per 100 years, an incomplete interval of at least 37 years is very likely. If the rate parameter were higher, say one even per 10 years, the likelihood of seeing the 37-year incomplete interval is very low.
Panel (c) puts together the data from the complete and incomplete intervals. The likelihood function in (c) is the product of the two likelihood functions in (a) and (b).
The amount of data available dictates how precise a statement is justified by the evidence. Statisticians often quantify precision in this context by using the \(\pm\) notation. For instance, an estimate of \(0.03 \pm 0.01\) would indicate “95-percent confidence” that the true rate parameter lies within the interval \(0.02\) to \(0.04\). In each of panels (a), (b), and (c) we have indicated this 95-percent confidence interval with the vertical magenta lines.
A good rule of thumb is that quadrupling the amount of data roughly halves the width of the confidence interval. But there is little reason to expect the new interval to be centered on the old estimate. The most one can say is that the new interval will probably overlap the original interval. That may be counter-intuitive, but uncertainty is sometimes that way!

text:
11.2 Putting numerical evidence into words
A likelihood ratio is a measure of the strength of evidence. In interpreting likelihood, verbal ideas like “weak” evidence, “moderate,” and “strong” turn out to correspond to the magnitude of the likelihood ratio, where “magnitude” is used in the sense of Chapter 5.
The translation of a continuous quantity into a small set of verbal descriptions necessarily involves imposing some breakpoints. Table 11.2 provides a widely accepted set of breakpoints for translating the magnitude of the likelihood ratio into a verbal interpretation.
