In accepting the verbal interpretations in Table 11.2 we are relying on the experience of past researchers. There’s nothing wrong with that. But it would be nice to have a definite interpretation of what “limited” or “moderate” evidence constitutes. The mathematics of likelihood provide a means to do this.
First, there’s general consensus among statisticians and scientists that a likelihood ratio of 10,000 is sufficient to satisfy the criterion for “strong evidence” in favor of a hypothesis. Now, imagine that your observations have yielded a likelihood ratio of 100. How much more evidence would you need to collect to reach a ratio of 10,000. One answer is, you can’t know for sure because you don’t know in what direction the new evidence will point.
But assume you are excited enough about your existing evidence to believe it will be worthwhile to continue collecting data. Your excitement leads you to suspect that the additional data will point in approximately the same direction as your current evidence. (But there is never a guarantee!) If your suspicion were correct, you would have to plan to double the amount of data you use to calculate the likelihood ratio. A nice way to do this would be to have some other researcher confirm your earlier results while doubling the amount of data overall.
Suppose you flip a coin 10 times and get 6 heads. Are you justified in believing the coin is biased toward heads? To answer this question, you need to compare two hypotheses. One hypothesis is that the coin is not biased, that is, the likelihood of getting a head is 0.5. Statisticians refer to such a “nothing-out-of-the-ordinary” hypothesis as a ☞ Null hypothesis ☜. You need another hypothesis to compare it to, a hypothesis that specifies what is the amount of bias. Let’s call this the “research hypothesis.”” For instance, you might consider a research hypothesis that the likelihood of getting a head is 0.6.
Under the Null hypothesis the likelihood of getting 6 heads and 4 tails is:
\[\underbrace{0.5 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.5}_\text{For the heads} \cdot \underbrace{0.5 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.5}_\text{For the tails} = 0.0010\]
Under the research hypothesis, the likelihood of getting 6 heads and 4 tails is:
\[\underbrace{0.6 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.6}_\text{For the heads} \cdot \underbrace{0.4 \cdot 0.4 \cdot 0.4 \cdot 0.4}_\text{For the tails} = 0.0012\]
The likelihood ratio comparing the research hypothesis to the Null hypothesis is 1.2. This provides no reason to favor the research hypothesis. But, like a detective hunting for the criminal, you can try to collect more evidence, that is, more data.
For fun, imagine a dialog with the chief investigator (your boss) and with a likelihood expert present:
Detective: Chief, I only have very preliminary evidence that the coin is biased (at 0.6), but I have a strong hunch and I’m sure it will become more convincing if I collect more data.
Chief: How much time have you spent on this?
Detective: Just two days. But enough to feel it in my gut that the coin is biased.
Chief: It would be nice to put this case to bed, one way or the other. Take another two days and update me then.
Detective: Will do. Thanks, Chief.
Two days later
Detective: I have been following up on the case. What I’m seeing is a match to my previous hunch, I think it’s more than a hunch.
Chief: Do you think you can wrap it up in another two days?
Detective: I’m confident.
Department Likelihood expert: Hold on. Your first two days investigation produced a likelihood ratio of 1.2. If your new data is consistent with your previous data, the combined likelihood ratio will be the square of 1.2, which is 1.44. If you were to spend another 4 days, the ratio would be 1.44 \(\times\) 1.44 = 2.07. That would be laughed out of court!
Chief: What would it take for the evidence to be convincing?
Department Likelihood expert: For evidence “beyond a reasonable doubt”, we would need a likelihood ratio of 10,000 or thereabouts. That would take about 100 days worth of data. And even after that, there’s no reason to think, at this point, that things would come out the way you want.
Chief: How much data would we need to convince the perp to accept a plea deal?
Department Likelihood expert: For a plea deal, the required likelihood ratio would be much lower, perhaps around 100 to 1000. We’re talking 50 to 75 days of evidence collecting.
Chief (to Detective): I want you off the case. We’ve got better things to do.

title: 12  Bayesian reasoning
text:
12.1 An uncertain situation
We are in the midst of a real-world experiment involving millions of people in a life-or-death situation. Perhaps that is an overly dramatic description. The experiment we have in mind concerns the testing of self-driving taxis in urban areas. Companies like Waymo have deployed fleets of self-driving cars that offer a taxi service.
That such testing is allowed is itself notable. How much experience will we need with the cars to be sure that we are making a proper judgment?
Companies currently run pilot programs deploying self-driving taxis in a handful of cities. They have already collected substantial amounts of data and reported summaries such as this Waymo bulletin. Instead of commenting on this data, let us imagine ourselves at the time when the safety experiment is just beginning. Then, we will gradually accumulate data to form and update our beliefs about fleet safety. We will keep it realistic, but because the data will be made-up, do not use this example to draw conclusions about the real world.
“Safety” is a dimension, an aspect of the transportation system. Modeling safety starts by defining it clearly, to operationalize it. Our operationalization in this discussion will be the number of miles driven by each car from the time it enters service until the first accident. We can define an “accident” as an incident that generates a claim on insurance or requires a police report. For other purposes, a different operationalization might be appropriate, for instance the number of close calls or near-misses
A car without an accident to date is not necessarily safe. Even accident-free cars provide information about fleet safety; the duration of the no-accident-yet interval carries that information. (See Figure 11.2.) A car that goes a large number of miles without an accident provides pro-safety evidence; A car that has an accident after a small number of miles does the opposite.
Chance influences whether a car is in an accident. This play of chance can be modeled with a probability distribution. An appropriate family of distributions for this was used earlier in Chapter 11: the exponential family. In Chapter 11 we used the time between incidents. For driving, the mileage of each car is a better representation of that car’s exposure to the risk of accidents.
Exponential distributions model the time interval, or mileage, in our case, between incidents. The interval here is the mileage from the start of the experiment until the first accident. For an individual car, this interval is modeled as random, a draw from the exponential distribution used to model the individual cars.
Even though each accident (or lack of accident) is random, the fleet safety plays a role. This fleet-level safety is operationalized by the particular rate parameter used for the individual-car randomness. The appropriate value for the rate parameter is uncertain. This uncertainty is large at the start of the experiment. As the experiment proceeds and more data arrives, the uncertainty will decrease.

title: 12  Bayesian reasoning
text:
12.2 The fleet-wide likelihood function
Fleet-safety uncertainty is a probability distribution on the rate parameter itself. Unlike individual-car uncertainty, this need not be exponential in form. At first, we don’t even know the proper form for the distribution should be. We will have to discover that form as we go along.
Suppose that at the end of each month the mileage and accident status of every car in the fleet are recorded. For any assumed value of the rate parameter, the likelihood of the observed data can be computed: multiply together the likelihoods for each individual car’s observed outcome.
The rate parameter is uncertain. Repeating the likelihood calculation for each possible value of the rate allows us to see how plausible each value is given the observed data. In other words, we create a likelihood function for the rate parameter.
Imagine that you are the person responsible for constructing the likelihood function that incorporates the latest data. You have a stack of cards, each recording the current mileage of an individual car or, if the car had an accident, the mileage at which the accident occurred. Each card’s information corresponds to an individual likelihood function for that car.
Plotting the individual-car likelihood functions requires choosing appropriate range of values for the rate parameter. Historical data on human-driven cars suggests a rate of about five serious accidents per million vehicle miles. A sensible plotting range is 0 to 40 accidents per million miles. The upper end lets you consider hypothetically very dangerous cars. The low end hypothesizes that self-driving cars are safer than human-driven. The middle hypothesizes that self-driving cars are about as safe as human-driven cars. Figure 12.1 shows three individual-car likelihood functions based on the most recent data for that car. The cars plotted in panels (a) and (c) have not yet had an accident. The car in (b) had an accident at mileage 78,954.











(a) 31,448 miles with no accident











(b) 78,954 miles with an accident













(c) 54,365 miles with no accident







Figure 12.1: Individual likelihood functions for several cars based on their mileage and accident status.



Consider the likelihood functions graphed in Figure 12.1. The two accident-free cars’ likelihood functions differ only slightly in shape.
The accident-free cars favor a low hypothesized rate parameter. Their likelihood functions peak at a rate of 0 accidents per million miles and fall steadily as the hypothesized rate increases. This evidence hardly proves that the cars are safe. Recall that a likelihood ratio of 10 is only “limited evidence” in favor of the more likely hypothesis. (See Table 11.2.) Only hypothesized rates where the likelihood falls below the magenta can be considered unlikely. So the accident-free cars don’t rule out a very high hypothesized rate of 40 accidents per million miles. This isn’t surprising, since the rate 40 per million miles amounts to an average of one accident every 25,000 miles! Reaching 54,000 miles isn’t shocking even under high risk.
The car in panel (b) experienced an accident. Its likelihood function has an argmax at a hypothesized rate of 12.7 accidents per million miles. This means an average of one accident every 80,000 miles, entirely consistent with the car having had an accident at 78,954 miles. This car only weakly argues against rates below 0.5 accidents per million miles.
Any individual car’s evidence does not precisely identify a specific hypothesized rate parameter. Each car here is entirely consistent with the historical rate for human-driven cars.
But your job is not yet complete. Combine the evidence from all the individual cars to assess what they have to say about fleet safety. Fortunately, this is easy. Just multiply the functions together. The result, from just these three cars is shown in Figure 12.2.








Figure 12.2: Combined likelihood for all three cars





Data from just three cars cannot resolve whether the self-driving cars are safer or more dangerous than human-driven cars. You need data from hundreds or perhaps thousands of cars.
Since individual-car likelihoods are weak on their own, you decide to adopt a work flow where, as you pick up each car’s data card, you immediately update the combined likelihood, by multiplying it by the new card’s likelihood.

title: 12  Bayesian reasoning
text:
12.3 The Prior
There’s a small technical glitch to take care of. The first card has no combined likelihood to multiply it with. Two simple work-arounds are available:

Use the likelihood function from the first card as the initial combined likelihood.
Start with a combined likelihood function of that is uniform, which effectively says “I have no prior evidence for one hypothesized rate over another.”

Note that (a) and (b) amount to the same thing. In practice you are starting out with the likelihood function from the first card. But designers already did substantial work to make the cars safe. For instance, the government approved the test cars for use on the public roads in the first place.
The Bayesian framework has a slot for inserting such before-the-first-data-card knowledge into the analysis. This is called the ☞ prior ☜ and reflects what you know before looking at the data. The “you” here is important. The experiment aims to convince others, no just yourself, that enough evidence exists for a meaningful conclusion. So the prior should reflect the beliefs of both the skeptic and the enthusiast.
US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg had a helpful view about debate. She said, “Fight for the things that you care about, but do it in a way that will lead others to join you.” One way to lead others to join you is to acknowledge the possibility that they might be right. In the Bayesian framework, this means broadening your prior to support the views of all (reasonable) people engaged in the debate. You do not have to assign much probability to those views, but you must assign some.
Sensible priors should be broad, not narrow minded. This point is not unique to quantitative analysis, but applies to reasoning and debate more generally.

To have doubted one’s own first principles is the mark of a civilized man. — Supreme Court Justice, Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr (1841-1935)


Doubt is an uncomfortable condition, but certainty is a ridiculous one. — Voltaire (1694-1778)


The whole problem with the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves, and wiser people so full of doubts. — Bertrand Russell (1872-1970)

title: 12  Bayesian reasoning
text:
12.4 The Posterior and Bayesian updating
Let’s re-consider the work-flow presented in the previous section. You started with an appropriately vague prior, then multiplied it successively by the likelihood from each data card as you picked it up. In the end, you have a distribution that reflects all the data. This distribution is called the ☞ posterior ☜, the state of your knowledge after taking all the data into account.
Calling the likelihood function from the first card L_1_() and so on for the subsequent cards, the posterior distribution after n cards is:
posterior() \(\equiv\) prior() \(\times\) L_1_() \(\times\) L_2_() \(\times\) … \(\times\) L_n_()
Since the prior() in the previous section was vague, perhaps even flat(), it’s reasonable to wonder why even to give it a name; just multiply the cards’ likelihood functions together. Indeed, for a hundred years statistical theory was dominated by exactly this point of view, named “Frequentist statistics.”
Consider, however, a slightly different scenario for processing the data on vehicle mileage and accidents. Rather than a batch of cards coming in all at once, suppose that they arrive sequentially, one by one. For the sake of definiteness, let’s assume that they arrive once per day and that the likelihood function for each day’s data is L_day_().
On day zero, before any cards arrive, all you have is your vague prior, which we’ll call prior_0_(). In comes the first card, day 1, and you perform your calculation, multiplying that day’s likelihood by the prior:
posterior_1() $L_1_() \(\times\) prior_0_()
On day two, the second card arrives. The Bayesian multiplication for day two will be
posterior_2() $L_2_() \(\times\) posterior_1_()
And for day three:
posterior_3() $L_3_() \(\times\) posterior_2_()
The general pattern is that yesterday’s posterior becomes today’s prior. The prior is your state of knowledge in the morning. The posterior is your state of knowledge after the day’s work is done.
Even if prior_0_() is vague, the prior for successive days will become less and less vague as more data is incorporated.
To illustrate, consider this dramatic example. A small ship has caught on fire. The crew has mere moments to send an SOS which includes a rough latitude and longitude for their location. “Rough” means that there is uncertainty.
The SOS is received by far-away radio stations. The content of the SOS contains the rough coordinates, but the direction from which the signal is received is also noted. These directions, one from each station help to define the search target.
Before the SOS, the Coast Guard’s prior for the sinking ship is more or less uniform, covering a broad expanse of ocean. (Indeed, the Coast Guard doesn’t yet know there is a sinking ship.)
Receipt of the SOS allows the Coast Guard to calculate a likelihood for the ship’s location based on the Coast Guard’s previous experience with the accuracy of such signals. Similarly, the direction-detecting equipment gives a likelihood function for the direction of the sinking ship relative to the Coast Guard’s stations’ locations. Multiplying these three likelihoods—from the SOS contents, and the two directions—allows the Coast Guard to calculate a posterior probability for the location where the ship sank. Figure 12.3 shows the posterior probability as a function of latitude and longitude.



Figure 12.3: Posterior probability for the ship’s location based on the SOS and direction-detecting equipment.










(a) Based only on the SOS content.











(b) Adding in directional data.








Anxious to find the ship’s crew, one of the Coast Guard stations sends out a search and rescue plane. It flies in a straight line toward the most likely location in Figure 12.3(b). It can be hard to spot a life raft from a quick-moving plane. Again, based on the plane’s course and the Coast Guard’s experience they can construct a likelihood for the plane’s finding the raft. This is shown in Figure 12.4(a).











(a) The likelihood for the plane to spot the life raft.











(b) The updated posterior probability after the plane’s flight.







Figure 12.4: Posterior probability for the ship’s location after incorporating directional data.



The plane complete’s its mission, but unfortunately it does not spot the life raft. Taking this information into account, the new posterior probability for the raft’s position is shown in Figure 12.4(b).
The sensible thing at this point is to send out another plane to fly another course. Your job is to decide what the course should be to maximize the chances of spotting the raft. The current posterior provides a lot of guidance here. What would you do?

title: 13  Dynamics: Modeling change
text:
13.1 The Euler framework
Section 1.5 introduced a model of an epidemic: the SIR model. SIR tracks the numbers of infective and susceptible people from day to day, week to week, and month to month. Such models, and the systems the models represent, are called ☞ dynamical systems ☜.
In simple language, a dynamical system is one that changes over time. A pendulum, swinging back and forth, is a dynamical system. A skyscraper shifting in the wind is a dynamical system. A flying airplane or rocket is a dynamical system. So are a building’s heating and cooling systems. Engineers and others often model these real-world dynamical systems to determine the strength, stability, and motion of the objects and, importantly, to design the control systems that govern their behavior. In a modern airplane, the pilot flies a model, and the control system brings the airplane into compliance with the model.
We have to be careful in understanding “changes over time.” The pendulum, airplane, and skyscraper are not changing; they are fixed mechanisms. It is their state that changes. The angle and speed of the pendulum bob oscillate up and down. An airplane’s control surfaces change with every whisper of air turbulence, and with them, the pitch, roll, and yaw of the plane change second by second. Builders may have installed a home heating system a decade ago; the “changes in time” consist of the furnace turning on and off in response to fluctuations in indoor temperature.
Historically, we can trace the mathematical foundations for modeling dynamical systems to the decades around 1700. The “Laws” of science are generally written in the language of dynamical systems. The earliest of these are Newton’s Laws, but much more modern frameworks—quantum physics, general relativity, electromagnetism, fluid mechanics—are all formulated in terms of dynamical systems.
We will consider only simple physical systems, such as the swinging pendulum, which suffices to lay out the mechanics of modeling dynamical systems. Mostly, we will emphasize theoretical dynamical systems used to model social, ecological, national security, and similar phenomena, such as epidemics. These theoretical systems are story-like descriptions, not intended to be taken literally as “laws.” Despite their approximations and simplifications, the theories serve as frameworks for developing understanding and anticipating the outcomes of interventions in real-world systems. Conveniently, for the person starting to learn what dynamical systems are, the theoretical systems allow a reader to work with familiar mechanisms, such as competition and disease transmission, rather than first having to learn the scientific esoterica of torque, angular momentum, viscosity, space-time curvature, quantum wave functions, and such. However, if the reader develops an interest in such things, he or she will already have a grasp on the mathematics shared by the scientific theories.
We will use the ☞ Euler framework ☜ for introducing the quantitative description of dynamical systems. The Euler framework involves three mathematical components:
As an example, consider the position of a ball dropped from a tower. At any instant, the ball’s altitude quantifies how far it has moved since it was released. The altitude is, of course, changing. The ☞ velocity ☜ is the rate of change of the position. Similarly, the output of the dynamical rule is the rate of change of the state.
Thinking of the picture in terms of a state space, the state at any instant is a position in the state space. The output of the dynamical rule is the direction and speed with which the state moves.
There are different ways to do the accounting. The methods traditionally taught in college-level math involve algebra that many students find daunting. The method we will use is arithmetical, invented by Leonhard Euler (1707-1783), one of the greatest mathematicians of all time.
The accounting method is entirely mechanical. To start, the user gives an initial state for the system. This state is fed into the dynamical rule which produces the instantaneous rate of change for the state, much like a “velocity” for the state. The method multiplies the velocity by a small time increment, producing a change of state, then adds the change to the initial state. This process of
\[\text{state} \ \rightarrow\  \text{change of state}\  \rightarrow\ \text{new state}\]
is repeated over and over, leading to a sequence of states: the trajectory of the system. The calculations involved are arithmetic, but tedious. Typically, software is used to do the work.
We will return to the accounting method and give it a dignified mathematical name in Chapters 14, 15, and 16. Since it is automatic, the modeler need not be particularly concerned with how it works. Think of it as an appliance, say, a toaster.
Dividing the mathematical work between the dynamical rule and the accounting method greatly simplifies the dynamical rule. The rule needs only to tell the change in the state over the briefest imaginable interval of time. This feature of dynamical rules enables the concise description of scientific theories of nature’s operation.

title: 13  Dynamics: Modeling change
text:
State

The ☞ State ☜ is a collection of one or more quantities that give a complete description of the instantaneous configuration of the system. It can be helpful to consider the instantaneous state to be a point in a space, just as we did in Section 3.7. We use the term ☞ state space ☜ as the set of possible states for a dynamical system.

Dynamical rule

The ☞ Dynamical rule ☜ specifies how the state changes over time. The dynamical rule is a function that takes a state as input and produces as output a description of the near future. That is, the dynamical rule tells, for each possible state, how the state changes over the next instant. Since the dynamical rule is a function, for each input there can be only one output value.





Accounting system

The dynamical rule tells how the state changes, but only over the next instant. Often, we want to trace the state’s movement over a substantial interval of time. The accounting system keeps track of the state’s instantaneous rate of change, accumulating it to compute the state as a function of time. This function is called the ☞ trajectory ☜ of the state.

title: 13  Dynamics: Modeling change
text:
13.2 Defining the state and rule
It is convenient to start with a system whose dynamical rule is straightforward and where we can easily keep the overall trajectory in mind. With this in mind, imagine a pendulum, such as a tire hanging by a rope from a tall tree branch, or the swinging mechanism of a grandfather clock.
Figure 13.1 shows the situation:






Figure 13.1: Animated drawing of a swinging pendulum. (Source])




The animation in Figure 13.1 consists of a series of frames. Figure 13.2 shows the first five frames individually, making it straightforward to measure the bob’s position in each.








Frame 1







Frame 2







Frame 3









empty







Frame 4







Frame 5






Figure 13.2: Five successive frames from the movie. The spacing between tick marks is 1 degree. Between frames 1 and 2, the pendulum is swinging slightly to the left. Thereafter, the swing is to the right.



What is the instantaneous state of the pendulum system? Let us start the discussion with a proposition (that will turn out to be wrong): the state is merely the position of the bob at each instant, as marked in the snapshots shown in Figure 13.2.
The position changes from frame to frame: \[7.2^\circ \rightarrow 6.3^\circ  \rightarrow  7.2^\circ  \rightarrow 8.9^\circ  \rightarrow 11.0^\circ  \rightarrow \ldots\ .\]
In both frames 1 and 3, the position is 7.2 degrees. Following frame 1, the position moves to 6.3 degrees, then back to 7.2 degrees for frame 3. Continuing in that direction, the position arrives at 8.9 degrees for frame 4.
Recall from Section 13.1 that a dynamical rule is a function. A function can produce only one output for each particular input. Consequently, the dynamical rule for a pendulum cannot produce two different outputs for the input state of 7.2 degrees.
Tempting though it might be to deal with this problem by allowing the dynamical rule to be something other than a function, there is a good reason for the (arbitrarily sounding) restriction, introduced in Chapter 6, that there be a unique output for any given input.
Instead of changing the framework, we need to redefine the state. For a pendulum, this change is straightforward: add another state component. An excellent way to do this is to add the bob’s instantaneous velocity to the state, so that the state space becomes the coordinate pair (position, velocity).
The markings in Figure 13.2 suffice to mark the position, but the individual frames say nothing about velocity. For velocity, we need to do a calculation. The position at frame 1 is 7.2 degrees, then 6.3 degrees at frame 2. So the change in position from frame 1 to 2 is \(6.3 - 7.2 = -0.9\) degrees. Velocity, however, is not just a change; velocity is a rate of change with respect to time.
The frame rate of the video in Figure 13.1 is 10 per second. That is, the time between successive snapshots in Figure 13.2 is 0.1 seconds. Consequently, the rate of change of position with respect to time—in other words, the velocity—from frame 1 to 2 is -0.9 / 0.1 = -9.0 deg per sec.
In contrast, from frame 3 to 4, the change of position is \(8.9^\circ - 7.2^\circ = 1.7^\circ\). The velocity over the 0.1 seconds between frames is therefore 17 degrees per second.
Defining the state as the pair (position, velocity) allows us to construct a dynamical rule that has a unique output for each state input.
Since the state has two components, the output of the dynamical rule must also have two components: the rate of change for each of the components in the state.
The rule for the first component is straightforward because the velocity is the rate of change of position. So the rule (in part) looks like this:
\[\text{pendulum\_rule(pos, vel)} \equiv (\text{vel}, \Large{\textbf{???}}) \tag{13.1}\]
We placed ??? in the slot for the rate of change of the “vel” component of the state in Math expression 13.1. The rate of change of the velocity—that is, the acceleration—is given by the physics of gravity, the extent to which gravity tugs with or against the current velocity. Still, we can model the acceleration as a function of position very simply. Recognize that at the very bottom of the pendulum’s swing—position 19—gravity is exactly countered by the vertical rod, so at position 19, the acceleration is zero. That lets us specify more of the dynamical rule for the pendulum:
\[\text{pendulum\_rule}(\text{pos}=19, \text{vel}) \equiv (\text{vel}, 0) \tag{13.2}\]
To construct a complete dynamical rule, we still need to generalize this to apply to any position, not just 19 degrees. A straight-line function of position will be a good start. We know the output of the straight-line function will be zero when the position is 19. By the argument in Note 13.1, the acceleration at position 7.2 is \(80^\circ \text{per sec}^2\). The linear function that connects velocity 0 at position 19 and velocity \(80^\circ \text{per sec}^2\) at position 7.2 is \(-6.78(\text{pos} - 19)\). Slotting this formula in place of the ??? in Math expression 13.2 gives the complete dynamical rule:
\[\text{pendulum\_rule}(\text{pos}, \text{vel}) \equiv \left(\text{vel},\  -6.78(\text{pos} - 19)\right) \tag{13.3}\]
Rules in this form are suitable for calculation, but to get a better understanding of how the system works, Figure 13.3(a) shows the state space with the two-component output of the dynamical rule drawn as a vector. The graphic displays the dynamical rule at only about 200 points in a row-and-column grid in state space. In reality, the dynamical rule applies to all points in the space. We cannot show them all because the graphic would become a solid mass of black arrows.
Applying the accounting method turns the dynamical rule into a trajectory. Figure 13.3(b) shows the trajectory. The initial state (time = 0) is marked 0. The other boxed numbers indicate the time (in seconds) at which the state reached that point.



Figure 13.3: The dynamical rule for the system of r('fig-pendulum-gif'). The rate of change at selected points in the state space is a vector since both components of the state are changing.










(a) Dynamical rule











(b) Trajectory








We draw the dynamical rule at the various points in the state space with a straight arrow. The arrow has two components, horizontal and vertical. Similarly, there is an instantaneous rate of change for each component of the state. The arrows show both instantaneous rates of change simultaneously. In contrast, the trajectory traces out the evolving state over a period of time: two seconds in Figure 13.3(b). The trajectory is a smooth curve. The accounting method does the mathematical work to turn the straight arrows of the dynamical rule into a curved trajectory.






Note 13.1: Estimating acceleration



We can estimate the acceleration at position 7.2 by examining the short three-frame movie \(6.3^\circ  \rightarrow  7.2^\circ  \rightarrow 8.9^\circ\). The velocity represented by the first arrow is, as before, \[\frac{7.2^\circ - 6.3^\circ}{0.1\ \text{sec}} = 9^\circ \text{per sec}\] Likewise, the velocity at the second arrow is \[\frac{8.9^\circ - 7.2^\circ}{0.1\ \text{sec}} = 17^\circ \text{per sec}\]
The acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity:
\[\frac{17^\circ \text{per sec} - 9^\circ \text{per sec}}{0.1\ \text{sec}} = 80^\circ \text{per sec}^2\]

title: 13  Dynamics: Modeling change
text:
13.3 The SIR model
A key feature of the Euler framework is that the dynamical rule describes the rates of change in the state only instantaneously. Although the trajectory may curve over extended durations of time, at each instant the dynamical rule needs to account for only a tiny change in the state corresponding to a small fraction of the vector. The accounting method moves this small amount, then evaluates the dynamical rule at the new state, then moves again, and so on. Any curve in the trajectory arises from repeated evaluations of the dynamical rule at state points that are very close together. Since the accounting method handles any curvature in the trajectory, the dynamical rule is much simpler than the extended trajectory.
We can now explore the dynamical rule for the SIR model of epidemics first presented in Chapter 1. To start, we need to specify the state of the SIR system.
A simple but effective representation of the state is two numbers: the number of susceptible people (\(S\)) at any instant and the number of infective people (\(I\)) at that instant.
To keep the model simple, we will not account for the infection’s origin. To start an infection, we set \(I\) to a nonzero value and let the dynamical rule take over.
To start, we will draw the state space and the dynamical rule at many individual points in the state space, as in Figure 13.4. Then we will interpret the dynamical rule in terms of familiar aspects of infectiousness and recovery from infection, and we will show the modeling techniques used to implement it.








Figure 13.4: The state space of the SIR model with the dynamical rule shown with arrows.





Figure 13.4 shows a state space suitable for tracking an epidemic in a population of 100,000 or fewer. At any instant of time, the sum of \(S\) and \(I\) cannot be greater than 100,000. So, we need only draw the dynamical rule in the area of state space where \(S + I < 100,000\), the lower triangular region of the state space.
The first thing to notice is that the dynamical rule arrows tend to have a leftward-heading component. The leftward trend indicates that \(S\) is decreasing; the model does not include the production of new susceptibles by birth or immigration.
In contrast, the rate of change in \(I\) can be either upward or downward. For low values of \(S\), the rate of change in \(I\) is downward because fewer people catch the disease than the number who are recovering from infection. Such recovery occurs at high \(S\) as well, but there the susceptible population is so large that many new individuals become infective.
We have marked a few state-space positions with colored dots to help us consider how the dynamics are different depending on \(S\) and \(I\).
The dynamical rule comes from the modeler’s knowledge of the system. Even those who may not have previously thought about the quantitative description of epidemics likely understand some basic principles.

New infectives are created when an existing infective meets a susceptible, converting the susceptible to an infective.
Existing infectives recover at some rate, lowering the number of infectives without changing the number of susceptibles.
If we ignore births, immigration, and deaths, as we are doing here, the only route for a change in the number of susceptibles is conversion via an infective.
All other things being constant, a larger number of infectives leads to a larger number of conversions of susceptibles. Similarly, all other things equal, a larger number of susceptibles results in more conversions.

These principles play out differently across regions of the state space, since the balance between susceptibles and infectives varies with position. Consider these (color-coded) regions in state space:
Few susceptibles, many infectives The flow is mainly southward, a little to the west. This corresponds to a slow decline in susceptibles as they run into any of the many infectives. Net decline in infectives: more are recovering than are being created by conversion of susceptibles.
 No susceptibles The flow is slowly to the south. No new infectives, but old infectives are gradually recovering.                       
A few infectives and many susceptibles  The flow is slowly to the northwest. This corresponds to slow growth in infectives and a corresponding decrease in susceptibles.
Many infectives and many susceptibles  The flow is rapidly to the west. This is a rapid decline in susceptibles.

text:
13.4 Trajectories














Figure 13.5: A chain of steps for the SIR model starting with \(S \approx 100,000\) and a handful of infectives. Each step covers 12 hours. The steps are plotted in alternating colors to make it clear where one step ends and the next one begins. The path indicated by the chain of steps is the trajectory of the dynamical system from the initial state.



In Figure 13.5, each step is a short line segment. The overall path accumulated through many steps, however, is curved. The curve is the result of re-evaluating the dynamical rule at the end of each short, simple step. Since the state moves only a small distance during one step, the output of the dynamical rule will be only slightly different when evaluated at the end of the step than it was at the start of the step. The overall trajectory, the accumulation of many small steps, approximates a gradual curve, just as we perceive smooth motion in a video, which is just one still frame after another. The time between the frames is very small, so successive frames are almost identical. The slight frame-to-frame difference produces the sensation of continuous motion.
Compare the trajectory in Figure 13.5 with the corresponding graph in Figure 1.1. They look completely different because the graphs are made in different spaces. In Figure 13.5 the axes are I vertically and S horizontally. But in Figure 1.1 the horizontal axis is time. The levels of I and S are both plotted along the vertical axis. The time of each position in the trajectory in Figure 13.5 is implicit and can be calculated by counting the number of steps needed to bring the state to that position. In contrast, Figure 1.1 shows the time is explicitly.

title: 13  Dynamics: Modeling change
text:
13.5 SIR dynamical rule
As mentioned previously, a dynamical rule is a function that takes the state as input and produces the instantaneous change of state as output. In Chapter 9, we introduced ways to build custom functions to represent a given situation. We are going to put those techniques to work, now.
The two state quantities in SIR are the number of susceptibles (\(S\)) and the number of infectives (\(I\)). Even without thinking much about the mechanism of epidemics, we can write down a skeleton form for the instantaneous rate of change. We will use the abbreviation ROC to stand for “instantaneous rate of change,” and the ROC of \(S\) will be named \(ROC_{S}()\) and likewise for \(I\). Both \(ROC_{S}()\) and \(ROC_{I}()\) will take the state \((S, I)\) as input. Each will be a linear combination of four simple functions.
\[ROC_{S}(S, I) \equiv a_s + b_s \, S + c_s\, I + d_s\, S\,I \tag{13.4}\] and \[ROC_{I}(S, I) \equiv a_I + b_I \, S + c_I\, I + d_I\, S\,I \tag{13.5}\]
The first thing to notice about the proposed functions in Expressions 13.4 and 13.5 is that they are almost the same. That might be surprising, since they describe the ROC of two different quantities, \(S\) and \(I\). Keep in mind that we are building a ☞ skeleton ☜ for the functions. We will flesh out the skeleton in different ways.
The “flesh” on the skeleton is the coefficients used in the linear combination. We combine four simple functions, so each expression has four coefficients. We have (uncreatively) named these coefficients \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), and \(d\).
We need a dynamical-rule function for each of the two state variables. For simplicity, we will use the same skeleton for each function, but endow each with its own flesh. That is, we will use different coefficient values for each dynamical rule. A simple notation helps make the skeletons’ similarities clear while at the same time signalling that the values of the corresponding coefficients in each skeleton can differ. We do this by adding a subscript, I or s, to each coefficient, depending on whether it is in the dynamical rule for the infectives or for the susceptibles. For instance, \(a_I\) is the coefficient on flat() for the \(ROC\_I\)-skeleton. Similarly, \(d_S\) is the coefficient on the interaction between \(S\) and \(I\) for the \(ROC\_S\)-skeleton.
Ultimately, we will want to give quantitative values for each of the eight coefficients \(a_s, b_s, c_s, d_s, a_I, b_I, c_I, d_I\).
Experienced modelers have a trick to facilitate the initial construction of a model. Rather than specifying a value for each coefficient, they state, based on their understanding of the system they are modeling, the sign for each coefficient: negative, positive, or zero. Going slightly further, they explore a limited set of scenarios: the state variables are either “large” or “small.” (The state variables in SIR cannot be negative, since there is no such thing as a negative number of infectives or susceptibles.)
Let us start with the coefficients in \(ROC\_I\).

\(a_I\): Think about what this term would indicate if both \(S\) and \(I\) were zero, the hypothetical world with no infectives or susceptibles. It seems reasonable to suppose that new infectives (that is, the rate of change of infectives) would not come out of the air. So \(a_I = 0\). 
\(b_I\): This is the coefficient on \(S\). Imagine that \(S\) is large, but \(I\) is zero. What will happen to the ROC of I? Without any infectives, there is no way for a susceptible person to become sick. So \(b_I\) must be zero. 
\(c_I\): This is the coefficient on \(I\). Imagine, contrary to the discussion of \(b_I\), that \(I\) is large and \(S\) is zero. In such a hypothetical world, there are no susceptibles who can become sick so that no new infectives will arise from the susceptibles. However, there is a mechanism for a change in \(I\) even when \(S\) is zero: Infectives can recover and stop being infectives. The more infectives there are, the larger the rate (say, infectives/day) at which they recover. In consequence, \(c_I\) is a negative number. Without susceptibles, the number of infectives decreases over time.
\(d_I\): The coefficient on the interaction term \(S\ I\) for \(ROC\_I()\). This is a case where standard nomenclaturee gets things right: “Interaction” is an excellent name for this term. A nice way to think about interaction is that it refers to what happens when an \(S\) meets an \(I\): they interact. With infectious illness, the possible outcomes of the interaction are either no change in the situation or, with some probability, the \(S\) catches \(I\)’s infection, and the \(S\) becomes infectious. So when an \(S\) meets an \(I\), the number of infectives increases. Thus, \(d_I\) must be positive; it is creating new infectives.

If the model is to allow influx of infectives from other places, the model would call for a positive \(a_I\).If the model is to allow spontaneous generation of infection, \(b_I\) would be positive.The analysis of \(a_s\), \(b_s\), \(c_s\), and \(d_s\) follows the same kind of logic. \(a_s\) would correspond to immigration of susceptibles (if positive) or emigration (if negative). The SIR model does not consider this. SIR also does not consider births or deaths. The number of susceptibles only changes when an \(S\) meets an \(I\). When that happens, the number of susceptibles decreases as susceptibles are converted into infectives. So \(d_s\) must be negative. What is more, since every susceptible individual who is infected becomes a new infective, it must be that \(d_s = -d_I\).
A nice convention when writing rate-of-change coefficients is to stipulate that all are positive. When a coefficient enters negatively into the rate-of-change function, we will use a minus sign instead of the \(+\) used in Equations 13.5 and 13.4
Taking into account all the coefficients that we argued are zero, we end up with two formulas for the rate of change functions:
\[ROC_{S}(S, I) \equiv - d\,S\,I\] and \[ROC_{I}(S, I) \equiv -b I + d\,S\,I\]
There are only two coefficients, not three, since the decrease in susceptibles balances any increase in infectives!

title: 13  Dynamics: Modeling change
text:
13.6 Exponential growth and decay
Demographers estimate that a fertility rate of 2.1 children per woman keeps the population steady; the number of births matches the number of deaths. In many wealthy countries, however, fertility rates are much lower. To dramatize the consequences, some pundits have extrapolated what would happen if the worldwide fertility rate were roughly one child per woman.
Assuming equal proportions of males and females, this low fertility rate results in half as many births in each generation as in the preceding generation. Over ten generations, successive halvings would result in the tenth generation having only one-thousandth as many births as the starting generation.
These successive halvings are an example of ☞ exponential decay ☜. Likewise, if the fertility rate were roughly four children per woman, the number of births would double every generation. These successive doublings, each taking approximately one generation illustrate ☞ exponential growth ☜. Demographers would put the rate for doubling every generation at 4.2 children per woman. Why? One reason is that not all of those children will themselves have children. Certainly, this is true of the boys, who constitute roughly half the population of child-bearing age. So, 4.2 per woman is 2.1 per person.
The phrase “exponential growth” appears often in the press, almost always in reference to a quantity growing rapidly, e.g., a population of insects or a national debt. The news media use synonyms for “exponential growth” to convey drama: skyrocketing, explosive, rampant, mushrooming, and so on.
The characteristic of all exponential growth is successive doublings, each taking the same time as the previous doubling. For example, at an annual compounding rate of 6%, it takes about 12 years for an investment to double. An investment starting at 1000 USD would grow to 2000 USD in 12 years, then to 4000 USD at the 24-year point, and to 8000 USD at the 36-year point. All forms of exponential growth work like this, whether they be about money, bacteria, growing vegetation, or anything else. They differ only in how long it takes for the doubling to occur. The ☞ doubling time ☜ is the parameter used to describe exponential growth.
Exponential decay is the same. Imagine an abandoned bank account with 1000 USD, where the bank takes a “service fee” of only 4% per year. At this rate, it takes the bank 18 years to extract half the account balance. So, an account with 1000 USD in 2000 will have only 500 USD by 2018, then 250 USD by 2036, then 125 USD by 2054, and so on. By analogy to the doubling time of exponential growth, exponential decay is characterized by a ☞ halving time ☜.
Some people point to the world’s human population (Figure 13.6) as a compelling example of “skyrocketing,” that is, exponential growth. However, a careful examination reveals a more nuanced story. After all, even skyrockets run out of fuel at some point.



Figure 13.6: Source: Our World in Data






To evaluate patterns like that shown in Figure 13.6, it pays to drop the dramatic descriptions and carefully examine what exponential growth is and the mathematical assumptions that underlie it. Knowing these assumptions lets us judge to what extent those assumptions are justifiable and when they are not.
We can start with dynamical systems that are, mathematically, extremely simple. What do we mean by “simple?” Two things: 1) the state space consists of just a single quantity, and 2) the dynamical rule is free from complexity. In honor of Figure 13.6, we will call the state quantity \(P\). (Of course, any other name would do: \(x\), pop, \(S\) for state, and so on.)
The simplest function in our core modeling collection is flat(), where the output is always 1 regardless of the input. We will start from there and gradually add complexity.
Figure 13.7 shows the dynamics of the flat() rule in three different ways. On top (panel (a)) is the flow field. In principle, since the state space is one-dimensional, all the flow arrows should be on the number line. To avoid the arrows overlapping, however, we have spread them out at random vertically. Panel (b) shows the dynamical rule, namely, the function flat(\(P\)). Panel (c) shows how the state \(P\) changes with time. (The name given to how something changes with time is ☞ time series ☜.)
Keep in mind the substantial difference between the dynamical rule and the corresponding pattern of how \(P\) changes with time, that is, the time series. The dynamical rule is a function that takes \(P\) as input and produces the rate of change of \(P\) as output. The time series is also a function, but instead of taking \(P\) as input, it takes time (t) as the input. Moreover, in the time series, the output of the function is \(P\) itself, not the rate of change in \(P\).



Figure 13.7: Flow field when dynamical rule is flat().










(a) Flow field











(b) Dynamical rule













(c) State vs time








The flow arrows tell a simple story. The flow is the same for every value of \(P\): steady, rightward movement. Tracking along the flow would give us P as a function of time, that is, the trajectory (panel (c)). The dynamical rule (panel (b)) corresponds with the flow: the rate of change of P with respect to time is constant. Of course, this is also what the trajectory shows: the rate of change of P with respect to time is constant.
A good name for the patterns in Figure 13.7 is ☞ steady growth ☜. A domestic example of steady growth is the accumulation of water in a bathtub as it flows in at a steady rate from the faucet.

title: 14  Rates of change
text:
14.1 Taxes on the margins
Chapter 4 introduced the distinction between a rate and a rate of change. A rate is one quantity divided by another. A rate of change is also a rate. But it is a special kind of rate.
The word “special” when talking about rates of change is relevant in two different senses. One definition is “different from usual.” Indeed if a rate is the usual thing, then a rate of change is different from usual because the quantities that form the ratio are always changes in a quantity. And not just changes, but simultaneous changes. By photographic analogy, you can measure a rate by looking at a snapshot: read off the instantaneous values of the two quantities of interest, then divide one by the other. In contrast, measuring a rate of change requires a movie: a series of instantaneous snapshots. The minimum length of the movie is small, just two frames. You measure the two quantities in one of the frames, then in the other. Take the change in each quantity between the two frames, then form a ratio of those changes.
Another meaning of “special” is captured by synonyms: exceptional, extraordinary, unique, important, significant, rare. Although the distinction between a rate and a rate of change may seem trivial at first glance, the invention of the concept (1600’s) and the gradual realization of the many important applications (starting about 1700 and speeding up over the next century and more) shaped many aspects of the modern world. This is most evident in science, technology, and engineering and the reason that a large fraction of STEM students are required to study rates of change and learn to do calculations with them. But it is just as important in economic matters, whether it be theories of how markets and firms work, or business decisions about prices and production.
Even if you have no interest in science, business, or economics, rates of change almost certainly apply to matters of importance to you. Knowing about rates of change, and how they are special, provides a major tool for understanding and making decisions about important matters. Later in this chapter, we’ll illustrate using death and taxes. First, though, let’s motivate the how and why of rates of change.
Income taxes in the US are calculated according to “brackets.” Each bracket specifies the tax rate, that is the fraction of income that is to be paid as taxes. Table 14.1 gives the brackets for taxes in 1913, the first year after the 16th Amendment to the US Constitution that empowered Congress to impose income tax.
In 1913, only about one-percent of households had an income of $3000 or greater, so taxpayers were a wealthy group of people.
Figure 14.1 shows lines 7 and 8 from the tax form for 1913. The form is blank, but we have filled in the numbers for a person earning the very large (in 1913) income of $90,000 per year.
Figure 14.1 is pretty confusing. There are a lot of numbers filled in. Ironically, even though the income is $90,000, that number does not appear on the form!
The 2024 tax table simplifies the calculation by giving a table. You need only look up your income. Figure 14.2 shows the appropriate entry from page 9 (of 11) of the closely-spaced pages. Less arithmetic, but still the income of $90,000 doesn’t appear.
A tax rate, as you know, is the fraction of income owed as tax. The tax table (Figure 14.2) does not indicate the rate, just the tax owed.
The quantities presented in the 1913 form in Figure 14.1 are not actually tax rates, although they look like it. In the form, they don’t even give a name to those quantities. The correct name is ☞ marginal tax rates ☜. A marginal tax rate is a rate of change; it compares a small change in income to the corresponding change in taxes owed. The tax policy expressed on line 8 of the 1913 form is a function: for any level of income, it tells the marginal tax rate for that income.
The advantage of specifying taxes in terms of marginal rates is two-fold. First, just a handful of numbers can convey the entirety of the matter. This is much easier to make sense of than the 11-pages of numbers given in the modern tax tables.
The second advantage is one of fairness, avoiding sharp breaks in the amount of taxes owed. Income $3000, taxes (in 1913) zero. Income $3001, taxes (in 1913) one cent, at least if marginal rates are being used. If the numbers gave overall rate, if it said that people with incomes of $3001 have to pay a tax rate of 1%, their taxes owed would be $30.01. A one-dollar increase in income leads to a $30.01 increase in tax owed. Stated another way, the take home earnings of the person with a gross income of $3000 is $3000. The take-home income for a gross income of $3001 will be $2970.99. Not very fair.
Author Charles Dickens expressed his concern about a lack of such fairness in the Victorian-era laws about debt. In David Copperfield, Mr. Micawber famously stated:
The overall principle here is that small differences in input should lead to small differences in output. In mathematical language, this is a principle called ☞ continuity ☜. In terms of the graph of a function, continuity means you can trace the function with a pencil without having to lift it off the table.
Having dealt with fairness in taxes, it is time to turn to fairness in deaths. First, however, we look at the meaning of “marginal.”

title: 14  Rates of change
text:
14.2 On the margin
The word ☞ margin ☜ comes from the Latin margo, meaning “edge.” On a printed book, the margins are at the edge of the text. “Marginal” is an adjective meaning situated on the edge of something else. When we talk about marginal income, the thing with an edge is the income itself. For instance, for the hypothetical person in 1913 with a $3000 income, the edge is at $3000. The marginal income sits at the edge; it is a small increment of income, say $1. The marginal tax rate is the rate that applies to that small increment, but not necessarily to the part of the income on the other side of the edge, the part below $3000.
In exploring systems whose state changes in time in Chapter 13, we considered rates of change of the state quantities. In particular, we worked with the concept of an instantaneous rate of change of state, the rate of change that applies for just an instant as the trajectory passes through each state in turn.
Marginal rate conveys the same sense as instantaneous, both are concerned with examining a tiny change on the edge of where you are. Of course, “instant” applies to time, while “marginal” applies to other kinds of quantities, for example income or expenditure or tax rate.
Economists often speak of ☞ diminishing marginal returns ☜. Consider, for instance, the situation of buying a car. They buyer is spending money and expects to get benefits in return: convenience and transportation services. For this, it suffices to buy the base model of the car. Many people go further, adding a marginal expense to buy an “options package,” with, say, heated seats and cruise control. In response to this marginal expense, the buyer anticipates getting a somewhat better car, that is, marginal benefits. But these marginal benefits are typically small in comparison to the benefits provided by the base model of the car. After all, by far the most important benefit of the car is providing transportaion services. When the ratio of the marginal benefits to the marginal expense is smaller than the benefit/cost ratio of the base model, one says that buying car options has diminishing marginal returns.
The next section looks at diminishing marginal returns in the context of setting health policy.

title: 14  Rates of change
text:
14.3 Competitive allocation
Many important matters in public and private decision making involve setting priorities. Compelling examples are provided by life-and-death issues. Consider this made-up setting which can illustrate important decision-making principles and is still somewhat realistic:

There are two innovations in public health care being considered. We will imagine them to be pre-natal clinic and improved cancer treatment, but give them very short names—“natal” and “cancer”—as a reminder that this is a made-up example.


The potential benefits from each innovation play out over the years. The Natal program will cost $5-billion, the cancer program $10-billion. Which one should the investment go to?

Different people can have different, reasonable views. Families of cancer victims will understandably place emphasis on the cancer initiative. People whose interests and lives center on young children might lean toward the natal initiative. Still others will advocate a compromise: split the $10-billion between both initiatives. And, inevitably, there will be another group who ask, “Why limit the budget to $10-billion? Fund both!”
The funding dilemma is an example of a trade-off. (Chapter 10) The new thing in this situation is that both objective functions—lives saved by spending on “natal” versus lives saved by “cancer” spending—are both quantified with the same dimension. But see the discussion of QALYs below.
The bald debate between advocates of spending on “natal” versus “cancer” does not point to a resolution. But since the objectives are measured in the same dimension, we do not need to think carefully about the “shadow costs” introduced in Chapter 10. Instead, it’s likely that the dualing advocates have a common goal: maximize the efficiency of the spending.
Consider briefly what should be the operationalization of the goals of the optimization problem. Perhaps it is obvious that a meaningful operationalization of the positive impact of each initiative would be the number of lives saved. Laudable though this be, this operationalization does not capture some important considerations. For instance, does deferring death for one day or one month count equally to deferring death for one year? “Number of lives saved” has dimension [1]. But [T] is also important.
A more nuanced operationalization is quality adjusted life years (QALYs). The “years” gives QALYs dimension [T].We will measure benefits in QALYs, but the same quantitative principles apply to other measures of benefit. And, since the reader is probably unfamiliar with QALYs, please accept for the purposes of discussion that QALYs are a better match to many people’s intuitive values than “lives saved.” Here are the (made-up) facts:

The Natal program will save 500,000 QALYs each year. The Cancer program will save 750,000 QALYs yearly.

Here are two quantitative arguments that lead to different outcomes:

The Cancer program saves more QALYs, so fund Cancer.
The Natal program costs $10,000 per QALY, while the Cancer program costs more: about $13,000 per QALY. Natal is a more economical choice.

Previous examples in this book have pointed out situations where rates, as in dollars-per-QALY, are more informative that single quantities. But it does not seem obviously wrong to favor the save-more-QALYs (a) argument over the save more dollars-per-QALY (b).
Arguments (a) and (b)—amount vs rate—are not the only way to compare the programs. Let’s consider one more useful quantitative perspective: rate of change.
In order to use rates of change, we need more information than provided above. We have to imagine that each program could be launched with a lower level of funding or perhaps even a higher level. Each potential level of funding corresponds to a QALY savings. Figure 14.3 shows two hypothetical functions: QALYs saved as a function of expenditure for the natal and cancer programs separately.



Figure 14.3: QALYs saved as a function of expenditure on each health initiative. The “facts” presented above are represented by the *. Plausible functions are sketched in for each initiative.

To start, we zoom in more closely to the domain near to the proposed funding level for each initiative. Figure 14.4 shows the competitive situation. In both graphs, the vertical scale covers 4000 QALYs; the horizontal scale covers $100 million.

Figure 14.3 shows that the slopes for the two programs are very different at the proposed expenditure levels. Figure 14.4 makes it easier to calculate the slope. For the Natal program, an increase in expenditure of $50 million corresponds to an increase in QALYs of 2,400. In contrast, for the Cancer program, a $50 million increase corresponds to only about 400 QALYs. The rate of change for Natal is \(\frac{2400}{50} = 48\) QALYs per $million. For Cancer, the rate of change is \(\frac{400}{50} = 8\) QALYs per $million.
The important implication here is that a million dollars is worth more QALYs if spent on Natal than on Cancer. This suggests that we should transfer money from Cancer to Natal. But how much?
Suppose we moved $5 billion from Cancer to Natal. The picture will look like Figure 14.5. The red stars mark the new spending proposal, re-allocating $5 billion from Cancer to Natal. Before rashly jumping to this conclusion, we should do a bit more analysis.
In Figure 14.5 we have annotated the graph with the rate of change (QALYs per million dollars) at the red proposal. This rate of change is, of course, the slope of the function at the selected expenditure level. We would need to do a little calculation to find the numerical value for the rate of change, but we can visualize it by drawing a line segment that has the same slope as the function at the selected expenditure level. The slope is steeper for Cancer than Natal, suggesting that we ought to shift money back to Cancer from Natal. This may seem futile, switching money back and forth, but that’s because we are shifting a lot of money: $5 billion. Suppose we shift less.
Whatever spending level we choose, there will be a QALY level marked by the star and a rate of change marked by the slope of the line segment. Figure 14.6 plots some of these line segments and stars at many different levels of expenditure.
