To the right of the “features” is a stack of four functions. Each function takes as input a linear combination of the f1(), f2(), …, f7() output values. The output of each of those four functions transforms the input so that the output ranges from -1 to 1.
As always, a linear combination is a sum of the form \[a_1 f_1 + a_2 f_2 + \cdots + a_7 f_7\], where \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_7\) are coefficients that determine the contribution of each feature. In Figure 16.7 the coefficients are displayed as dashed curves. The color of each curve indicates whether the coefficient is positive (blue) or negative (orange). The width of each curve is proportional to the size of the corresponding coefficient.
Ultimately, the input to the four functions is the x-y coordinate of the corresponding row of the data frame. The output—as a function of x-y position—is shown by the color in the small square representing each of the four functions. You can see that the four functions are more complicated than the original feature functions. Next in the display is a stack of two neurons. These take as input a linear combination of the outputs from the four neurons to the left. Again, the coefficients for this linear combination are displayed by the color and thickness of the dashed curves leading into the two neurons.
Finally, the outputs of the two neurons are combined linearly to produce the overall function shown in the larger square to the right of the two neurons. Since there are only two neurons being combined, its easy to read the coefficients in the final linear combination from the graph. The top neuron has a small, slightly negative coefficient. The bottom neuron has a stronger negative coefficient.
Focus now on the large square display on the right side of the graphic. As mentioned before, the individual rows of the data frame are represented by dots. The end-function implemented by the seven features and the six neurons is shown by the background color in the square. That end-function is intended to be a classifier for new data, that is, to take any x-y coordinate as input and provide as output the predicted class (i.e., orange or blue) for that coordinate.
As you can see, the neural network has learned enough about the pattern in the data to provide a reasonable classification for any new x-y coordinate. The orange dots lie in the orange area of the end-function: likewise, for the blue dots.
None of the original features resemble the pattern of the data points. Yet the coefficients of the various linear combinations turn these features into an end-function that captures the data pattern. How did that happen?
In abstract, we can say that the neural network was trained on the data from the data frame. Here, the goal of training is to establish the value for each of the coefficients in the network.
We can count the coefficients that have to be determined during training. Each of the seven features provides an input to each of the 4 neurons in the first hidden layer, resulting in \(7 \times 4 = 28\) coefficients. Each of the 4 neurons in the first hidden layer provides an input to each of the 2 neurons in the second hidden layer, resulting in \(4 \times 2 = 8\) coefficients. Finally, each of the 2 neurons in the second hidden layer provides an input to the single output neuron, resulting in \(2 \times 1 = 2\) coefficients. In total, there are \(28 + 8 + 2 = 38\) coefficients that need to be determined during training.
Here’s how the training works. To start, the coefficients are set to 38 random values. Naturally, the resulting function is unlikely to capture the pattern in the data. The training process looks at the function output for each of the dots in turn. Suppose the output from the initial end-function for row 1 of the data frame is 0.37 which can be translated to words: slightly blue. Since row one is actually in the orange class, the function provides an incorrect prediction. The goal of training is to adjust the coefficients so that the end-function gives a more appropriate output for row 1 (and all the other rows in the training data).
The end-function, as we’ve said, has 38 coefficients. The output of the end-function depends on each of these coefficients. We can differentiate the end-function with respect to each coefficient, producing a gradient vector in the 38-dimensional space of the coefficients. If we changed the coefficients slightly in the direction of this gradient, the output of the end-function would increase slightly. That would make the end-function output worse with respect to the data in row 1 of the data frame. To make the end-function output better, we simply need to change the coefficients slightly in the opposite direction of the gradient.
This change in the 38 coefficients might make the output of the end-function better or worse with respect to the other rows of data. The training process repeats this adjustment for each row in the data frame, each repetition making the end-function output slightly better with respect to that row.
The observed behavior of this iterative adjustment process is, very gradually, to improve the overall performance of the end-function with respect to all the rows in the data frame.
Consider now the upper right corner of the display, shown here.  This shows the progress of the training over time, as each successive move is taken along or opposite to the gradient. At each step, the “training loss,” that is, the total error of the end-function is calculated. Over thousands of adjustment steps, the training loss fluctuates up and down but overall, decreases. When further adjustment steps don’t reduce the training loss, the training algorithm stops, giving us the best set of 38 coefficients that was found.
The interactive, online version of the demonstrator shows the training process over time. As training proceeds, you can observe at each step the current end-function and how it changes in response to the adjustments of the coefficients. The behavior is very complex, yet it amounts to many, many steps along the gradient vector.

title: 16  Moving Past Two Inputs
text:
16.5 Space exploration
Chapters 11 and 12 introduced vectors in two-dimensional space, where simple tasks can be performed intuitively. For example, to measure the length of a vector, use a ruler! To find out whether two vectors are parallel, just look!
Now we want to extend our capabilities into higher-dimensional space. The motivation for this is, for example, making sense of complex data or constructing a model of language.
We start with three-dimensional space, where the geometry can be conveyed by moving the viewing perspective. This will let us explore how pairs of vectors can be used to specify a unique ☞ plane ☜. This leads to a new operation, ☞ projection ☜, which casts the shadow of a vector onto another vector or onto a plane.
The projection operation is key to working with data, for instance, building statistical models or identifying patterns in the data. But projection is especially powerful when working in high-dimensional spaces.
In four- and higher-dimensional spaces, it is practically impossible to draw a meaningful graphic. But the operations we can see in three dimensions can be calculated in any dimension using arithmetic. This includes vector length, angles between vectors, and projections onto planes or higher-dimensional extensions of planes.
To build intuition, let’s return to 3-dimensional space. Consider Figure 16.8, which shows two vectors, one in blue and the other gray. They are drawn on a green background. At a glance, one can see that the angle between the vectors is obtuse, perhaps about 130 degrees. Also, the gray vector is shorter than the blue vector. Easy!
In fact, each vector is 3-dimensional. And the green “background” is actually a plane that contains both the vectors. Try rotating the scene to see this more clearly.











Figure 16.8: Two vectors: blue and gray. You can position the cursor over the scene and press/drag to rotate the vectors in three dimensions.



As you change the viewing perspective in Figure 16.8, the apparent lengths of the vectors as well as the angle between them can change. And, you’ll see that the green “background” is actually a plane, with both vectors contained in the plane.
Indeed, if you change the perspective to view the plane edge-on, the blue and gray vectors will appear to lie on the same line. And depending on which angle you take (keeping the plane edge on), the two vectors will be arranged variously in opposite directions or in the same direction.
To measure the proper length of a vector, you need to lay down a ruler on top of the vector, parallel to it. Similarly, the measure the proper angle between the two vectors, you need to lay a protractor in the green plane that contains both vectors.
We can represent the situation arithmetically. Since the vectors live in three-dimensional space, the tip of each vector can be written in (x,y,z) coordinates. (For simplicity, the base of each vector will always be at the origin, that is, (0,0,0).) We could have put tick marks along the x-, y-, and z-axes to let you measure the coordinates of each vector, but for convenience, here they are.
\[ \color{blue}{\vec{v} \equiv \left(\begin{array}{c}7\\4\\0\end{array}\right)}\ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ \color{magenta}{\vec{w}\equiv\left(\begin{array}{c}1.5\\-4\\0\end{array}\right)}\] Note that, for future reference, we have given names, \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{w}\) to the two vectors.
With the arithmetic representation, we don’t need a ruler to measure the ☞ length of a vector ☜; the Pythagorean formula does the job.
\[\color{blue}{\sqrt{7^2 + 4^2 + 0^2} = 8.06}\ \  \text{and}\ \ \  \color{magenta}{\sqrt{1.5^2 + 4^2 + 0^2} = 4.27}\ . \tag{16.2}\]
We won’t do very much arithmetic here. But for what we will do, it will help to have a much more concise notation. Here are two parts of that notation:

A function, called the ☞ dot product ☜ which involves simple multiplication and addition. Here’s an example, the dot product between \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{w}\): \[\vec{v} \odot \vec{w} = 1.5 \times 7\ + \ -4 \times 4\ +\ 0 \times 0 = -5.5 .\] The dot product takes two vectors as input and produces an ordinary number as output.

Sometimes it is helpful to dot a vector with itself. For instance:
\[\vec{v} \odot \vec{v} = 7^2 + 4^2 + 0^2 = 65\ \ \ \] and \[\ \ \ \vec{w} \odot \vec{w} = 1.5^2 + (-4)^2 + 0^2 = 18.25\ .\]
This use of the dot product captures a large part of the Pythagorean formula for vector length (Math Expr 16.2).

The length of \(\vec{v}\) is written \(\|\vec{v}\|\). There is a simple formula for the length of a vector that uses the dot product:

\[\|\vec{v}\| = \sqrt{\ \strut\vec{v} \odot \vec{v}\ }\ \ \  \text{and}\ \ \  \|\vec{w}\| = \sqrt{\ \strut\vec{w} \odot \vec{w}\ }\ .\] This dot-produce notation pays off with slightly more elaborate calculations. For instance,

The ☞ alignment between two vectors ☜ is calculated like this: \[\text{alignment}(\vec{v}, \vec{w}) \equiv \frac{\ \ \ \ \vec{v} \odot \vec{w}}{\sqrt{\strut\ \|\vec{v}\|\ \|\vec{w}\|\ }} \tag{16.3}\]

title: 16  Moving Past Two Inputs
text:
16.6 Spaces with dimension greater than 3
Understandably, people have difficulty visualizing scenes in 4- or higher dimensions, or even imagining that such scenes might exist. Our cognitive abilities are tuned to perception in the familiar 3-D space of everyday life.
With the arithmetic representation of vectors, however, it’s easy to see how to construct vectors in 4-space, 5-space, or any-dimensional space. A vector in such a space is merely a column of numbers. Here are a few examples.
\[\color{magenta}{\vec{a} \equiv \left(\begin{array}{r}1.5\\3.0\end{array}\right)}\ \ \ \ \ \color{green}{\vec{b}\equiv\left(\begin{array}{r}4.2\\-7.1\\2.3\end{array}\right)} \ \ \ \ \ \color{blue}{\vec{c}\equiv\left(\begin{array}{r}0.3\\4.1\\1.9\\-3.2\end{array}\right)}\] \[ \ \ \ \ \ \color{purple}{\vec{d}\equiv\left(\begin{array}{r}1.0\\ -7.0\\  2.9\\  1.2\\ -4.1\end{array}\right)} \ \ \ \ \ \color{green}{\vec{g}\equiv\left(\begin{array}{r}-0.1\\ -8.8\\ -4.6\\  6.5\\  5.2\\ -4.2\end{array}\right)} \ \ \ \ \      \]
The count of components in each vector tells the dimension of the space where the vector exists or “lives in.”
The reader may object. “Of course, you can make a column of numbers with as many components as you like. What does that have to do with ‘space?’”
What makes these simple columns of numbers into an “object in space” is the calculations we can do with them, for instance, the “length” of a vector or the alignment between two vectors. Both of these calculations are rooted in the dot product, whose formula is a simple extension of that already shown. For instance, here’s a dot product in 5-dimensional space:
\[\color{olive}{\left(\begin{array}{r}1.0\\ -7.0\\  2.9\\  1.2\\ -4.1\end{array}\right)} \odot \color{black}{\left(\begin{array}{r}2.6\\8.3\\6.4\\1.6\\2.7\end{array}\right)}= \text{ }1.0 \times 2.6 \ -\ 7.0 \times 8.3\ +\ 2.9 \times 6.4 \ +\ 1.2 \times 1.6 \ -\ 4.1\times 2.7 = -46.09\]

title: 16  Moving Past Two Inputs
text:
16.7 Alignment, projection, and decomposition
Three important spatial operations in modern technology are

Finding the alignment between two vectors.
Defining a ☞ subspace ☜ of a larger space. As you will see, subspaces are a way of encoding information about patterns.
☞ Projecting ☜ a vector in the larger space down into a subspace. Since subspaces encode patterns, projection determines to what extent a vector displays those patterns.

The alignment quantifies how similar the two vectors are, that is, whether they have information in common. An alignment of 1 indicates that the vectors share all information. An alignment of zero means that they have no information in common. (An alignment of -1 means that the vectors share information completely, but that one vector has been reversed in direction.) The reader who has studied statistics may recall the “correlation coefficient.” This is essentially the same as the alignment.
In a two-dimension space, a subspace is a line: an infinite set of points that all lie within the bigger space. The line is a one-dimensional subspace. In three-dimensional space, there are two different kinds of subspaces: a line (1-dimensional) and a plane (2-dimensional). In higher-dimensional spaces, say one with \(n\) dimensions, there can be 3-, 4-, and up to \((n-1)\)-dimensional subspaces.
A one-dimensional subspace is defined by a single vector. A two-dimensional subspace is defined by two vectors.3 Similarly, an \((n-1)\)-dimensional subspace is defined by \(n-1\) vectors.
Figure 16.9 shows a two-dimensional subspace (that is, a plane) of the three-dimensional space. The two vectors drawn in the same color as the subspace have been used to define the subspace. We have colored the subspace-defining vectors to be inconspicuous, so the reader can focus attention on the subspace itself.








Figure 16.9: A two-dimensional subspace of a three-dimensional space. The black vector is not in the subspace.




You can verify that the two green vectors are in the subspace by rotating the scene. Whatever way you rotate it, you will never see the tips of the green vectors outside of the subspace. The black vector, however, does not lie in the subspace. (Of course, the green vectors must be in the subspace. We defined the subspace using the two green vectors.)
Projection of a vector onto a subspace means to find a new vector in the subspace that is a close as possible to the vector being projected. Figure 16.10 shows the projection of the black vector onto the green subspace. We have drawn in gray the “new” vector, that is, the one that lies in the subspace and is as close as possible to the black vector.








Figure 16.10: The black vector consists of a part entirely within the subspace and a part entirely outside the subspace.




To confirm that the gray vector really is the one in the subspace that is as close as possible to the black vector, observe these facts by rotating the scene:

The gray vector is in the green subspace. No matter how you rotate the scene, the gray vector never emerges from the subspace.
The tip of the black vector is directly above the tip of the gray vector. Admittedly, it can be hard to be sure of this just by observing the co-movement of the black and gray vectors.

To allow greater precision of observation, we have added a red that is perpendicular to the green subspace. You will want to confirm that this statement is accurate. Do so by rotating the space until you are looking at the subspace edge on. Whichever such perspective you take, the red vector will be perpendicular to the vestigial line of the subspace.
Now rotate the space so you are looking straight down the red vector. When you have this right, the red vector will look like a single dot. You will also see that the tip of the gray vector is exactly covered by the tip of the black vector.
Go back to looking at the subspace edge on. You should be able to see the black, red, and gray vectors. Notice that if the red vector were moved so that its base is at the tip of the gray vector, it would reach directly to the tip of the black vector. That is,
\[{\color{darkgray}{\text{gray}}} + {\color{red}{\text{red}}} = \text{black}\ .\]
Writing a vector as a sum of two other vectors is a form of decomposition. This decomposition of the black vector involves a part directly in the subspace (gray) and a part entirely outside the subspace (red).
In three-dimensional space, this is just fun and games. But in higher-dimensional space, where we need to perform the projection using arithmetic, it is the core technique of statistical modeling, a method that underlies many published scientific findings and that gives a more nuanced view of relationships than the simple rates described in Chapter 4.

title: 16  Moving Past Two Inputs
section: 16.8 Example: Learning to identify different species
text:
16.8 Example: Learning to identify different species
We are going to take on a ☞ learning ☜ task: figuring out how to classify the species of a penguin. For people, such learning comes from experience. Spend enough time with penguins, and you’ll figure out how to discern one type of penguin from another.
Consider now the problem of getting a computer to discern the different species from one another using physical measurements. Our motivation here is to demonstrate a process of learning. I don’t know that there is a practical, ecological motivation behind this problem.
In this learning task, we will start by sending human experts out to collect data from penguins: the species, but also quantitative data such as the penguin’s mass, beak length, and width, and so on. The data collected constitute a ☞ training data set ☜ that we will use to establish quantitative rules for identifying a penguin’s species.
Figure 16.11 shows training data from 344 penguins across three species: Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. Each penguin is one dot in the picture. The judgement of the human experts about the species is indicated by the color of the dot: Adelie is blue, Chinstrap green, and Gentoo red. Five different quantitative measurements were taken for each penguin, so the dots rightfully belong in a five-dimensional space. But we can only show three dimensions graphically, so we work with those.








Figure 16.11: Representing the penguin data as points in space.




From the perspective shown initially, it’s easy to distinguish the Chinstrap penguins from the other two species. But the Adelie and Gentoo species are all mixed up; we can’t divide the space into distinct regions that separate one species from another.
Now rotate the scene until each of the three species occupies a distinct region. By rotating, you are determining how to combine the various measurements to obtain the cleanest results from the training data. Once that learning has been accomplished, you’ll know how to classify any new penguin that comes along without a species label.
Think about how you learned the pattern. You rotated the space more or less at random, keeping track of which perspective best separates the groups of different-colored dots. Such a perspective optimization can also be automated, without human involvement. In fact, that is how the subspace shown in Figure 16.11 was determined. The information about species corresponds to the pattern encoded by the subspace.
This was a pretty easy learning task since it can be done in three dimensions. The next example demonstrates a more impressive feat performed in a space of more than 100 dimensions. What’s more, there is no expert providing the training data; the method will figure out how to perform classification without knowing the goal!

title: 16  Moving Past Two Inputs
text:
16.9 Example: Voting patterns
In high-dimensional space, random vectors tend to have an alignment close to zero. This is an important clue to help us spot patterns in data. As described previously, patterns are encoded by a choice of subspace. To search for patterns, we look for subspaces where projecting onto the space tends to produce vectors that are more closely aligned.
To avoid unnecessary abstraction and the mystique that can arise from leaving the familiar realm of three dimensions, we have selected an easy-to-understand setting: votes by legislators in a council. In particular, we will examine a series of 773 votes by 135 lawmakers in the Scottish Parliament in 1999-2000.4 This might seem an obscure topic, but the advantage for us is that few readers will have direct knowledge of the parliament’s political structure, for instance, the number and make-up of political parties. Similarly, the reader will not know how the 773 recorded ballots are related to one another.
This is an example of ☞ unsupervised learning ☜. In supervised learning, as with the penguin species assignment, we have training data about the patterns we seek to uncover: the different colored points in Figure 16.11 that enable us to find an advantageous projection onto a low-dimensional subspace. In unsupervised we have no such knowledge. The problem is then to find a low-dimensional subspace without knowing in advance what we are looking for.
To orient the reader, consider some of the data for one of the 135 members of parliament, Bruce Crawford. Mr. Crawford voted “For” 235 ballots, “Against” 264, and didn’t register a vote in 274. For instance, Bill S1M-786 was entitled “Ethical Standards in Public Life.” Mr. Crawford was in favor, as were 98 of his colleagues. (It is likely that most members of parliament are in favor of ethical standards in public life, but evidently, 17 members objected to something or another in the bill. There were 2 abstentions and 16 absences.)
A diligent researcher can read through the minutes of Parliament, which record which party each member belongs to and the content of each bill. But, in the spirit of unsupervised learning, we will not use this information.
Figure 16.12 shows the votes and absences for each of the 134 members of parliament on each of the 773 bills, giving somewhat over 100,000 data points. Each point is one member voting for or against one bill (or abstaining or being absent). The point’s color shows whether the vote was for or against.








Figure 16.12: Votes by 134 members of the Scottish Parliament on 773 bills considered in the 1999-2000 session. The “Ethical Standards” bill is column 183. Mr. Crawford is row 100.






Our goal is to find and interpret patterns in the data. There are many ways to define “pattern.” For instance, the reader will, possibly, see the overall pattern in Figure 16.12 as a plaid, a common fabric pattern. (Satisfyingly, plaid is culturally associated with Scotland, although that has nothing to do with the matter at hand.) Here, however, we will stick with the sorts of patterns that can be seen through the lens of quantitative reasoning, particularly the alignment of vectors and the detection of low-dimensional subspaces that provide a good approximation to the raw data.
We start with alignment, a useful measure that can be calculated using the formula in Math Expr 16.3, which involves simple arithmetic. We start by measuring the alignment among the various members of parliament. For each of the 133 members of parliament, we have a vector of votes on the 773 bills. For example, Bruce Crawford’s voting record is represented by the vector we have named \(\vec{M}_{100}\) in Math Expr 16.4. We also show vectors for a randomly selected few of his colleagues: Colin Campbell (\(\vec{M}_{99}\)), Paul Martin \(\vec{M}_{57}\), and Scott Barrie (\(\vec{M}_{25}\)). Each of the vectors has 773 components; we’re leaving out most of them for human readability.
\[\vec{M}_{100} = {\small\left(\begin{array}{r}1\\-1\\-1\\1\\1\\1\\1\\-1\\\vdots\\-1\\-1\\1 \end{array}\right)}\ \ \ \
\vec{M}_{99} = \small{\left(\begin{array}{r}-1\\1\\1\\-1\\-1\\-1\\-1\\1\\\vdots\\1\\1\\0 \end{array}\right)}\ \ \ \
\vec{M}_{57} = \small{\left(\begin{array}{r}1\\-1\\-1\\-1\\1\\1\\1\\-1\\\vdots\\0\\0\\0 \end{array}\right)}
\vec{M}_{25} = \small{\left(\begin{array}{r}0\\0\\0\\0\\0\\-1\\1\\1\\\vdots\\0\\1\\0 \end{array}\right)}\ \ \ \
\tag{16.4}\]
Note that the first component of all the vectors in Math Expr 16.4 corresponds to the vote on the same bill, S1M-1, and similarly for all the other bills up to S1M-4064.
Observe that \(\vec{M}_{100}\) is almost entirely the opposite voting pattern of \(\vec{M}_{99}\). To find the quantitative alignment, first take the dot product of the two vectors, \[ (-1) \times 1 + (-1)\times 1  + 1 \times (-1) + 1 \times (-1) + \cdots = - 8\] then divide by the square root of the lengths of the two vectors, \(\sqrt{11}\) and \(\sqrt{10}\) respectively. This arithmetic operation gives an alignment of -76%.
The point here is not to emphasize this particular calculation, but to show that the alignment is a straightforward statistic to compute. And, in any event, we should take into account all 773 bills when computing the alignment between two members of parliament. Table 16.1 shows the result.

Another way to look at the voting data is as 773 vectors, each having 134 components. That is, we make 134 measurements on each of the 773 bills. Looking at the alignments among the 773 vectors lets us organized the bills into blocks (Figure 16.13).
Figure 16.13 shows the entire data set from Figure 16.12 with both the rows and columns re-arranged to enhance the “blockiness” of the data.








Figure 16.13: The same data as in Figure 16.11, but the rows and the columns have been reordered so that closely aligned vectors are placed nearby along the axes.





The strong block structure in Figure 16.13 is evident. Looking across the columns, there are four factions. The largest, by far, includes the members numbered 60 and higher. The second largest faction consists of members numbered 1 through 36. This second faction is distinguished from the first by voting “for” bills 1-230 and against bills 580+. They also have many absences for bills 450-550.
Having identified two major factions, we can compare the voting patterns of members of parliament who are not in either faction. A third faction, contrasting with the first two, occupies 37-55. Meanwhile, a small fourth “faction,” rows 56 to 59, is a mix of opinions and absences.
To facilitate further discussion, let’s call the three substantial factions the “Top,” “Middle,” and “Bottom.” It turns out, by referring to the known party registration of each MP, the Top faction consists of a mix of Scottish Labour and Scottish Liberal Democrats, the Bottom faction is the Scottish National Party, and the Middle faction is the Scottish Liberal Democrats. The party registration information, however, played no role in the construction of Figure 16.13.
With these names for the horizontal bands in Figure 16.13, we can discuss the vertical bands: the types of bills considered by Parliament. Bills 1 to 230 have the Top faction voting “for” and the Bottom faction voting “against.” Bills 231 to 325 are opposed by both factions. Bills numbered 600+ are opposed by the Bottom faction but supported by the Top faction. Bills 326 to 450 receive support from both factions.
This is a lot to find out about a session of Parliament from a set of 100,000 “for” and “against” votes. It is not, of course, everything to know about the session. For instance, although we have identified four types of bills, we would need to read the actual bills or the debate record to determine which social, economic, or administrative features characterize each type. Here, modern quantitative reasoning provides a tool that can inform other types of description and argument.

title: 16  Moving Past Two Inputs
text:
16.10 Toward AI
Starting about 2015, the quantitative methods described in this chapter were combined to create the ☞ Large Language Models ☜, which helped launch the AI revolution. These approaches include:

Gradient ascent for setting optimal parameters.
Representing words and word contexts as vectors in high-dimensional spaces.
Finding projections that collapse words and their contexts so that sets nearby geometrically are also similar semantically.

This chapter does not equip the reader to use such methods in practice. Realizing current AI capabilities required many billions in research on quantitative methods. Researchers also discovered new quantitative methods, unknown to previous generations. For example, the 2017 paper Attention is all you need made a major step toward effective AI.
Readers who are daunted by the richness of the quantitative concepts in this book should keep in mind that mastery comes only after years of study and effort. This is true across many fields, including the humanities, medicine, the social sciences, and engineering. Even experts of one decade can be challenged by innovations in the next. For instance, this author has not yet understood the “Attention” method enough to describe it or outline its key ideas.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.1 Chapter 1: Models
Quantitative argumentation uses quantitative models to strengthen everyday reasoning, support decisions, and connect real-world situations with formal reasoning.
Reasoning transforms givens—–facts, observations, beliefs, assumptions, or knowledge—–into new beliefs or conclusions. Heuristic reasoning is broadly useful but not guaranteed; formal reasoning is reliable when its rules are applied correctly.
A model is a representation of an object, process, or setting. Models serve as bridges: heuristic reasoning helps construct a model, which then becomes the givens used for formal reasoning. .
Models are not intended to match the endless complexities of the real world. Instead, a good model captures essential features of the world in a way that is useful for reasoning and decision-making. Modeling is the iterative process of creating, testing, and refining models to improve their usefulness.
The example of the SIR epidemic model illustrates how a verbal account of a system can be translated into quantitative bookkeeping that supports simulation and the exploration of possible interventions.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.2 Chapter 2: Systems
A system is a structure of interconnected elements. In this book’s account of modeling, each element is a feature or dimension of the system.  In a quantitative model, dimensions are represented by quantities.Chapter 3 will introduce another, closely related meaning for “dimension” in the context of quantities
Operationalization is the procedure used to translate a dimension into a measurable quantity. Operationalizations do not necessarily capture all aspects of a system, they can be a compromise between the modeler’s mental image of a dimension (example: “comfort”) and the practicalities of measurement. Modelers should check that a dimension’s operationalization adequately represents the intended aspect of the system to suit the purpose intended for the model.
A value is the specific numerical level of a quantity, together with its appropriate unit. A changing value does not necessarily mean that the dimension or its operationalization has changed. For instance, the temperature of a room may change from 20°C to 22°C, but the dimension (temperature) and its operationalization (measured in °C) remain the same.
Data are recorded facts, findings, or measurements. A data frame organizes such data into rows and columns: each row represents a specimen of a common object type, each column represents a system dimension, and each cell contains a value.
A sample is a collection of specimens drawn from a larger population; relationships observed in data are collective properties inferred by comparing multiple specimens to one another.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.3 Chapter 3: Quantities
A quantity combines a pure number with units and, optionally, a description of what is being measured.
Dimensions describe the kind of quantity being measured; units are standardized ways of measuring it. Multiplying or dividing base units produces derived units, while dimensional analysis tracks the corresponding relationships among dimensions.
Dimensional analysis was invented originally for work in science, especially physics and engineering. But it is useful for quantitative work generally. For such general work, this book adds the dimensions “worth” [W] and “people” [C] (for “capita”) to the standard scientific base dimensions of length [L], mass [M], time [T], and thermodynamic temperature [Θ]. The square brackets, as in [T], can be read “the dimension of ….” (Other scientific dimensions—electric current [I], amount of substance [N], and luminous intensity [J]—are not used in this book.) We will also consider the dimension of pure numbers [1] as discussed below.
A pure number is a number without any associated units. It is useful to consider pure numbers as having their own dimension, denoted [1] in the bracket-format used in the chapter. This allows pure numbers to be treated consistently within the general dimensional analysis framework for quantities. Using the word “dimensionless” to refer to the dimension [1] is standard.
Quantities can be added, subtracted, or compared only when they are commensurate, meaning they have the same dimension. Unit conversion puts commensurate quantities into a common unit; a conversion factor, or “flavor of one,” is a dimensionless ratio of equal quantities whose units show the direction of conversion.
A quantitative change is the to value minus the from value, so it can be positive or negative. It compares a primary quantity across a context-setting quantity (such as time), expressed as change with respect to that context. The dimension of a quantitative change is that of the primary quantity. . A partial change examines one context-setting quantity while holding others constant.“Rates of change” (Chapter 4) are different. Their dimension reflects both the primary quantity and the context-setting quantity.
A space represents a collection of quantity types; a set of possible values. The space for a single quantity is a number line. Two quantities together form a coordinate plane. Larger collections form higher-dimensional spaces. Each point in the space a value for each of the quantities that make up the space.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.4 Chapter 4: Rates
A rate consists of one quantity divided by another and is an important way of describing the relationship between two dimensions.  The division is signified by the word per.“Dimensions” here refers to attributes of systems.
Being a quantity, a rate has units and is of the corresponding dimension. “Dimension” here refers to the type of quantity the units measure.
A conversion factor, or flavor of one, is a dimensionless ratio of equal quantities. But even though a conversion factor is dimensionless, it has units. The units determine the direction of conversion: to convert from one unit to another, use units of to/from.
A rate of change compares a change in a primary quantity with the corresponding change in a context-setting quantity. It is a rate, so its units identify both what is changing and what that change with respect to.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.5 Chapter 5: Magnitudes
Order of magnitude provides an alternative way of representing a number that is well suited when comparing numbers that differ by large factors. Magnitude describes the size of a number by focusing on the position of its first nonzero digit relative to the decimal point. Numbers that differ by factors of ten differ by one order of magnitude; numbers that differ by factors of 100 differ by two orders of magnitude.
Unit prefixes and scientific notation make magnitude easier to see without counting zeros. In scientific notation, the mantissa gives the digits and the exponent gives the approximate magnitude.
A logarithm provides a more precise, single-number representation of magnitude by incorporating both the mantissa and exponent. This book uses base-10 logarithms because they correspond directly to decimal scientific notation.
Logarithms apply only to pure numbers. Before comparing quantities with logarithms, convert them to the same unit; the units do not belong inside the logarithm.
Magnitude-based comparisons and graphics are useful when quantities span large ranges and the relevant comparison is a ratio. For quantities that differ by small amounts, such as ordinary changes in temperature, height, or blood pressure, direct differences are often more informative.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.6 Chapter 6: Functions
Recall that systems are collections of interconnected elements. A function is an important way to represent such a connection. A function takes as input one or more quantities and produces as output a single quantity. (By using multiple functions, we can represent more complex relationships and interactions within a system.)
The process by which a function turns the inputs into its output is called an algorithm. The several functions on calculators correspond to algorithms; you invoke the algorithm with a button press. The computer programming notation to invoke a function is different: the function name followed by parentheses containing the values for inputs, for example sultriness(temperature=28, humidity=0.75).
When a modeler creates a new function, she does so by putting together existing functions. (See, e.g., Chapter 9 for more on building complex functions from simpler ones, such as the core modeling functions introduced in Chapter 7.)

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.7 Chapter 7: Core modeling functions
As a set of basic building blocks for constructing more complex functions, this book selects eight core modeling functions. Each core modeling function gives a name to a simple functional pattern—a shape that relates a single input to the output.
Each core modeling function is like a simple plot in a collection of stories. Putting those plots together creates a richer narrative that captures more complex relationships within a system.
Every core modeling function takes a single pure-number input and produces a single pure-number output. We use input scaling to translate a dimensioned quantity into a pure number suitable for the core function. Similarly, output scaling translates the pure-number output back into a quantity with meaningful units.
that provide simple, reusable patterns that capture common types of relationships in quantitative models. A core modeling function is a named, reusable relationship that transforms one pure-number input into one pure-number output. The chapter provides a small library of eight simple functions whose shapes commonly occur in quantitative models.
The graph of a core function shows how its output changes as its input changes. The input and output are read from the grid, and the function’s shape provides a qualitative story about the relationship: constant, steadily increasing, oscillating, rising and falling, or changing at an increasing or decreasing rate.
The eight functions are same(), flat(), hill(), hillside(), exp2(), log2(), recip(), and osc(). Their names help communicate the relationship they represent and make the functions easier to use in computer implementations.
Input and output scaling translates the pure-number input and output of a core function into quantities with meaningful units. Shifting and stretching the axes preserves the function’s shape while adapting it to a particular modeling situation.
A modeler can use a core function as a starting pattern, then scale and interpret it for a real system. The chapter illustrates this process by modeling global oil production with exponential growth and by using familiar temperature stories to interpret each function’s shape.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.8 Chapter 8: Uncertainty
Often, a quantitative value is uncertain. Such uncertainty is an important feature of the quantity and needs to be represented formally. A simple way to communicate the amount of uncertainty is with a range: a lower and upper value.
A probability distribution is a richer and more reliable way to represent uncertainty. There are differently shaped probability distributions to reflect different patterns of uncertainty. A probability distribution is a function whose input is a possible value and whose output indicates how likely that value is relative to other possibilities.
The chapter introduces three useful distribution families: the uniform distribution for equally possible values within a known range, the normal distribution for values concentrated around a mean with decreasing likelihood farther away, and the exponential distribution for waiting times or other quantities with greater uncertainty toward the high end. (There are many more families used by modelers. This chapter focuses on these three.) One selects a specific probability distribution from a family by choosing appropriate parameters that specify its shape and scale.
Simulation is a useful computational technique that propagates uncertainty through a a system by randomly sampling inputs from their probability distributions, applying the system functions, and examining the resulting collection of outputs.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.9 Chapter 9: Composing functions
Just as a music composer can put together individual notes to form a melody, a modeler can put together simple functions (such as the core modeling functions) to compose a more complex representation of a system.
The chapter emphasizes two main ways of composing functions: multiplication, which captures interactions between quantities, and linear combinations, which capture additive effects of multiple influences. There are many other ways to compose new functions, which we don’t consider in any detail.
A linear combination of functions adds scaled functions. The scaling is accomplished by simple multiplication of the function with a number, called a coefficient. In general, coefficients are conversion factors that translate the units of the original function’s output into the desired units for the combined function.
Linear regression uses data to select good coefficients in a linear combination. The coefficients selected in this way are called regression coefficients.
Regretably, conventional introductory statistics courses cover only one simple aspect of regression (calling it “simple regression”) which amounts to what we are calling output scaling of a single function. But combining multiple functions, especially functions with different inputs, is a core quantitative technique throughout the social and natural sciences called “multiple regression.” Multiple regression is a foundation for understanding complex systems through data. One use of multiple regression is to model partial change (Chapter 3) and is associated with phrases like “after adjusting for …” or “controlling for …” or “holding other variables constant.”

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.10 Chapter 10: Tradeoffs
A tradeoff occurs when a decision-maker must balance competing objectives. Optimization provides a way to compare possible choices using an objective function, whose input is a possible choice and whose output measures the consequence of that choice in terms of the objective.
The argmax is the input that produces the maximum output of an objective function; the argmin produces the minimum output. A single objective function can identify a mathematically best choice, but that choice may be poor if the function omits other goals that matter.
When several objectives conflict, their outputs may have different dimensions and cannot simply be added. With multiple objectives, each policy choice produces an output from each objective function. Those several output values can be plotted as a point in the objective space; a space with an axis for each output objective. A graph of the objective outputs can identify choices that are dominated, meaning another choice is at least as good on every objective and better on at least one. Dominated choices can be eliminated; the remaining choices represent genuine tradeoffs.
A shadow price quantifies the exchange between competing objectives. It expresses how much of one objective must be given up to gain more of another, helping decision-makers clarify whether a proposed trade is worthwhile within real-world resource constraints.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.11 Chapter 11: Likelihood
A hypothesis is a claim about something, that might be off target to a greater or a lessor degree. The modeler’s understanding of how a system works, together with relevant data, inspire the modeler to formulate a hypothesis about how a system works, and a model is a formal implementation of such a hypothesis.
Likelihood is a quantitative measure of how well a hypothesis accounts for observed data. It is constructed by composing a probability distribution function corresponding to uncertainties in a model. The output of that probability distribution is a probability.  The input to the function is the entire set of observations/data.Technically, this may be a probability density. This book sidesteps that technicality When a hypothesis asswith the concept of relative probability.
Likelihoods are meaningful only in comparison to each other. The simplest comparison concerns competing hypothetical hypotheses for a parameter or set of parameters. Each parameter value corresponds to a specific probability distribution. The same input—the entire set of observations/data—is used as the input to the probability distribution function for each of the parameter values, one at a time. A likelihood function maps each parameter value to the likelihood of the observed data under that parameter value.
A likelihood ratio compares the support for one hypothesis to the support for another. If the likelihood ratio is greater than one, the hypothesis in the numerator of the ratio is preferred to the hypothesis in the denominator. However, likelihood ratios should be much greater than 1 to constitute any evidence at all for the preference. Likelihood ratios greater than 1000 provide strong evidence. A likelihood interval (much the same as a “confidence interval” in classical statistics) describes a range of parameter values that are well-supported by the observed data.
The likelihood depends on the amount of observations/data available. Collecting more data generally narrows the interval—quadrupling the data roughly halves the width of the interval—though it need not center the new estimate at the old one.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.12 Chapter 12: Bayes
Bayesian reasoning provides a way to translate a likelihood function into a probability distribution that takes into account other information, such as prior knowledge or beliefs, that is outside the observations/data used when evaluating the likelihood function. The resulting probability distribution is called a posterior probability distribution for the set of hypotheses under consideration (such as the possible values for a parameter).
The prior is a probability distribution function whose input domain is the set of hypotheses under consideration. The prior assigns a relative probability to each hypothesis, reflecting the degree of belief in that hypothesis before observing the data. The likelihood function reflects only the observations/data, not the prior belief.
Multiplying the prior function by the likelihood function produces the posterior function, which is the updated state of belief after taking into account the observed data.
There can be reasonable disagreement about the best choice of a prior, just as there can be reasonable disagreement about beliefs in general. A sensible analysis considers the extent to which the posterior is influenced by the specific prior selected. The more the observations/data, the less the influence of the prior; evidence overcomes prior belief.
At any point, a prior or a posterior can be multiplied by a number without changing their meaning. A favored normalization is to select the number such that the resulting distribution sums (or integrates) to one, ensuring it is an absolute (not relative) probability distribution. (See Chapter 15).

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.13 Chapter 13: Dynamics
“Change” will be the main theme of Chapters 13, 14, and 15. Up to now, we have emphasized “with respect to” change, for instance a system like A -> B where a change in A produces a change in B. Here, A is an exogenous quantity whose change is determined outside the system, while B is an endogenous quantity whose change is determined by the system.
Another important perspective on change comes from a system where the connections between elements form a loop. A simplistic example is A -> B -> A. This is simplistic because it doesn’t specify which comes first, A or B: A chicken and egg problem.
We can avoid this ambiguity by inserting an intermediary in the form of a system element describing the “change in A with respect to time.” For example:
A -> B -> ‘change in A with respect to time’
This is called a dynamical system and turns the exogenous quantity A in A -> B into a quantity whose change is determined within the system.
The Euler framework represents such a system with three components: the state, a dynamical rule that gives the state’s instantaneous rates of change, and an accounting system that accumulates those changes into a time-based trajectory.
A new graphics representation helps visualize the situation. The state quantities themselves (A and B in the above) are represented by a state space which has a dimension for each state quantity. The instantaneous state is represented as a point in this space. The change of state (the “change in A with respect to time” in the A -> B example) is represented as a vector originating from that point. The length of the vector indicates the speed of change, what we call the instantaneous rate of change.
A model of a dynamical system assigns a vector to each point in the state space; that vector is a function of the position of the point, that is, the values of A and B. This collection of vectors is called the dynamical rule or, informally, the “flow field.”
Following the flow produces a trajectory, the sequence of values taken up by the state quantities as they change with respect to time. A trajectory may be curved even though each individual vector is straight.
Exponential growth or decay arises from system where the change in the state is proportional to the current state, for instance, A -> ‘change in A with respect to time’. Perhaps surprisingly, such simple systems with multiple state variables can exhibit not just exponential behavior but also oscillations.
In a finite world, exponential growth cannot continue indefinitely. This truth emphasizes that models are always approximations which may not include all factors that eventually become relevant.

title: Appendix A — Chapter Summaries
text:
A.14 Chapter 14: Rates of change
A rate of change compares simultaneous changes in two quantities, for instance, how B changes with respect to A.
It turns out to be useful to consider instantaneous rates of change, which looks at how B changes with respect to a very small change in A. “Very small” can be treated as common sense; a change that is barely noticeable. There is also a mathematical abstraction which formalizes the idea of an infinitesimally smallchange change in A and its corresponding infinitesimally small change in B. Mathematics courses such as calculus tend to emphasize the abstraction, but for practical purposes the “barely noticeable” change is often sufficient.
The system A -> B can also be described as a function B(A), where A is the input and B is the output. The derivative of a function is a new function that gives the original function’s instantaneous rate of change. We might name this function change_in_B(A), but there are a variety of mathematical notations for it such as \(\partial_A B(A)\) where \(\partial_A\) means “change with respect to A of ….”  Differentiation is the process of calculating a derivative, and calculus is the broader field that studies this relationship. The derivative has the same input as the original function but a different output and dimension.Calculus students will recognize \(\frac{dB}{dA}\) or \(\frac{\partial B}{\partial A}\) which emphasizes that the derivative is a rate of change, but obscures that the derivative is a function of the with-respect-to input.
In economics, business, and most other disciplines outside of math and physics, the term marginal rate is used instead of “instantaneous rate of change” but has the same meaning of purtaining to a small, incremental change. Marginal tax rates, for example, describe the additional tax owed on a small increase in income rather than the average tax owed on all income.
Tradeoff situations, with two objective functions, have two rates of change with respect to the input policy quantity. The ratio of these two rates of change is effectively the rate of change of one objective output with respect to the other objective output. This can be interpreted as a shadow price. An optimization example about health care in the chapter seeks a balance between two health programs at a point where the marginal benefit per dollar spent is equal across the programs.

A.15 Chapter 15: Accumulation
Accumulation is the process of finding a total from a rate of change over an interval. When the rate is constant, accumulation is calculated by multiplying rate by duration; when the rate changes, the same idea is carried out by integration, or anti-differentiation.
An accumulation function and its rate-of-change function contain the same information in different forms. The rate-of-change function is the derivative of the accumulation function, while the accumulation function is the anti-derivative of the rate. An initial value is needed to determine the vertical position of the accumulated function.
The relationship between marginal and total quantities can make models easier to construct and interpret. For example, a marginal tax-rate function can be accumulated to obtain total tax owed. Similarly, modeling QALYs saved per additional dollar can be easier to justify than directly modeling total QALYs saved; accumulation then produces the total-benefit function.
Accumulation is also at the core of the accounting system used in the Euler framework for dynamical systems.
The chapter illustrates this framework with population data. Rather than extrapolating the population time series directly, modelers can estimate how the population’s rate of change varies with population or time, then accumulate that rate to forecast future population. This approach makes the model’s assumptions visible and provides a basis for checking whether predicted growth or decline is plausible.

A.16 Chapter 16: Toward higher dimensions
Many quantitative problems involve finding inputs that produce a desired output or maximize an objective. When the function cannot be graphed or described algebraically, a modeler can estimate local rates of change and walk uphill by taking small steps in a direction that increases the output.
For a function with several inputs, the gradient is a vector made from the rates of change with respect to each input. It points in the direction of steepest ascent. Repeatedly evaluating the gradient and taking small steps produces a practical gradient ascent algorithm for optimization, even when the function has thousands or millions of inputs.
Vectors provide a way to represent points, directions, and data in spaces with any number of dimensions. The dot product can be used to calculate vector length as well as the angle of alignment between two vectors. Alignment measures similarity: positive alignment indicates similar direction, zero indicates no shared direction, and negative alignment indicates opposing direction. AI systems use such alignment to quantify similarlity of meaning, allowing them to exploit patterns of meaning expressed in different terms.
A subspace is a lower-dimensional structure within a larger space. Projection represents a vector by the closest vector in the subspace, separating the part of the data captured by a pattern from the remaining residual. These operations provide the mathematical foundation for statistical modeling and for finding patterns in high-dimensional data.
The chapter illustrates supervised learning by using labeled penguin measurements to identify species and unsupervised learning by finding voting patterns without using party labels or bill descriptions. Reordering and projecting high-dimensional voting data reveals factions and types of bills, showing how quantitative methods can discover patterns that require other forms of reasoning to interpret.
